120970.q: What is the disadvantage of a higher ultrasound frequency?
120970.e: High frequencies give finer detail but are damped more strongly in tissue. So lower frequencies are used for organs lying deep inside.
120970.m: High ultrasound frequencies show detail but do not reach as deep.

120971.q: What advantage does ultrasound imaging have over X-rays and computed tomography?
a: It passes through bone especially well
It shows the air in the lungs best
120971.e: Ultrasound is a mechanical wave, not high-energy radiation. So the examination is considered gentle and can be repeated as often as needed.

120972.q: Why are air-filled lungs and bones hard to examine with ultrasound?
a: Because they reflect or damp the sound almost completely
Because they turn the ultrasound into light
Because they move too much during the measurement
Because their cells contain no water
120972.e: Air and bone have a very different acoustic impedance from soft tissue. So the ultrasound can hardly get behind them, and an acoustic shadow forms.
120972.m: Behind air and bone, ultrasound shows a shadow.

120973.q: What does a diversity index measure in ecology?
a: The number of species and how individuals are distributed among them
Only the total number of all individuals
The biomass of the largest species
The area of a nature reserve
120973.e: A diversity index combines the number of species and the evenness of the distribution of individuals in a single number. Two communities with the same number of species can therefore differ in diversity.
120973.m: A diversity index takes into account the frequency distribution as well as the number of species.

120974.q: What is the simple number of species in an area called?
120974.e: Species richness only counts how many species occur. How common each species is does not matter.
120974.m: Species richness counts the species without considering how common they are.

120975.q: Which term describes how evenly the individuals are distributed among the species present?
120975.e: Evenness (equitability) is greatest when all species are equally common. If one species strongly dominates, evenness is low.
120975.m: Evenness measures how evenly the species are distributed.

120976.q: What does the Simpson index D, as the sum of the squared proportions (Σ p²), indicate?
a: The probability that two randomly drawn individuals belong to the same species
The average body size of the species
120976.e: If you draw two individuals at random (with replacement), Σ p² is the probability that both belong to the same species. A high value therefore means low diversity.
120976.m: A high Simpson value Σ p² means that a few species dominate.

120977.q: A meadow has three species with proportions of 0.5, 0.25 and 0.25. What is the Simpson diversity 1 − Σ p²?
120977.m: You get the Simpson diversity by subtracting Σ p² from 1.

120978.q: According to Robert Whittaker, what is the diversity within a single habitat called?
120978.e: Whittaker distinguished alpha diversity (within a habitat), beta diversity (difference between habitats) and gamma diversity (whole region).
120978.m: Alpha diversity describes the variety at a single site.

a: The difference in species composition between habitats
The number of species in a whole region
The genetic variety of a species
The number of individuals per square metre
120979.e: Beta diversity measures the species turnover between sites. If two meadows have completely different species, it is high.
120979.m: Beta diversity measures how much habitats differ in their species.

120980.q: Which three levels of biodiversity are usually distinguished?
a: Genetic diversity, species diversity, ecosystem diversity
Cell diversity, organ diversity, species diversity
Plant diversity, animal diversity, fungus diversity
Climate diversity, soil diversity, water diversity
120980.e: Biodiversity includes the variety of genes within species, the variety of species and the variety of habitats and ecosystems. This is also how the Convention on Biological Diversity defines it.
120980.m: Biodiversity includes genes, species and ecosystems.

120981.q: What does the Shannon index measure in ecology?
a: Species diversity, taking into account how common each species is
Only the number of species in an area
The total biomass of an area
The growth rate of a population
120981.e: The Shannon index takes into account not only how many species occur but also how evenly the individuals are distributed among them. The higher the value, the more diverse the community.
120981.m: The Shannon index combines the number of species and how common they are.

120982.q: Which field does the Shannon index originally come from?
120982.e: Claude Shannon developed the measure in 1948 as entropy in information theory. Ecology later adopted it as a measure of diversity.
120982.m: The Shannon index comes from Claude Shannon’s information theory.

120983.q: What is the Shannon index (natural logarithm) for two equally common species?
120983.e: With p = 0.5 for both species, H = −2 · 0.5 · ln 0.5 = ln 2 ≈ 0.693.
120983.m: For S equally common species, the Shannon index equals ln S.

120984.q: What is the Shannon index of an area where only a single species occurs?
120984.e: With p = 1, ln 1 = 0, so H = 0. A monoculture has no diversity in the sense of the index.
120984.m: A single species gives a Shannon index of zero.

120985.q: For a given number of species S, when does the Shannon index reach its maximum?
a: When all species are equally common
When the number of individuals is at its maximum
120985.e: With equal proportions, the uncertainty about which species you will draw next is greatest. The maximum is then Hmax = ln S.
120985.m: The Shannon index is greatest when species are equally common.

120986.q: What does the evenness of a community describe?
a: How evenly the individuals are distributed among the species
How many species occur in total
How large the area studied is
120986.e: Evenness, for example according to Pielou, compares the measured Shannon index with the maximum for equally common species. It lies between 0 and 1; 1 means that all species are equally common.
120986.m: Evenness shows how evenly the species are represented.

120987.q: Two meadows each have three species. In meadow A all species are equally common; in meadow B one species makes up 90 per cent. Which meadow has the higher Shannon index?
a: Both the same, as the number of species is the same
Meadow B, because one species dominates
120987.e: For the same number of species, the Shannon index is highest when all species are equally common. If one species strongly dominates, the index falls considerably.
120987.m: Unequal proportions push the Shannon index below its maximum.

120988.q: What is the maximum Shannon index (ln) for four species?
120988.e: The maximum is ln 4 ≈ 1.386. It is reached when each species has a proportion of 0.25.
120988.m: The highest possible Shannon index is the natural logarithm of the number of species.

120989.q: Who coined the concept of biodiversity hotspots in 1988?
120989.e: The British environmental scientist Norman Myers described areas with many endemic plants and severe habitat loss in 1988. Conservation International later developed the concept further.
120989.m: Norman Myers invented the concept of biodiversity hotspots in 1988.

120990.q: What does it mean if a plant species in a hotspot is endemic?
a: It occurs naturally only in this area
It was brought in by humans
It is found all over the world
120990.e: Endemic species exist only in a particular area. Hotspots have especially many of them, so losing them there would be irreplaceable.
120990.m: Endemic species occur only in a particular area.

120991.q: Apart from having many endemic species, which second criterion must a biodiversity hotspot meet?
a: It has lost at least 70 per cent of its original vegetation
It lies completely in the tropics
It is larger than one million square kilometres
120991.e: Hotspots are not only especially rich but also especially threatened. That is why at least 70 per cent of the original habitats must have been lost.
120991.m: A hotspot is rich in species and at the same time severely threatened.

120992.q: Where are most of the Earth’s biodiversity hotspots?
a: In the deserts of Central Asia
120992.e: Most hotspots are in warm regions with many endemic plants, such as the tropical Andes, Madagascar or South-East Asia. Habitat loss is also great there.
120992.m: Most hotspots are in the tropics and subtropics.

120993.q: What proportion of the Earth’s land surface do the hotspots still cover (intact vegetation)?
120993.e: The remaining intact habitats of the hotspots cover only about 2.5 per cent of the land surface. Even so, more than half of all plant species live there as endemics.
120993.m: A large part of plant diversity is concentrated on a tiny part of the land surface.

120994.q: Which of these areas is a recognised biodiversity hotspot in Europe?
120994.e: The Mediterranean Basin is a hotspot because of its many endemic plants and its long use by humans. It is one of the largest in the world.
120994.m: The Mediterranean Basin is Europe’s best-known biodiversity hotspot.

120995.q: Why were hotspots proposed as a tool for nature conservation?
a: To use scarce funds where the most species per area can be saved
To steer tourists into nature reserves
To count the number of species worldwide exactly
120995.e: The concept helps to set priorities: investing in hotspots protects many irreplaceable species on a small area. Critics complain that animals and less species-rich ecosystems lose out.
120995.m: Hotspots help to use conservation money as effectively as possible.

120996.q: Which island, together with neighbouring islands, is a hotspot of its own and famous for its lemurs?
120996.e: Madagascar separated from other land masses over 80 million years ago. This produced a great many endemic species, including all the lemurs.
120996.m: Madagascar is a hotspot with an extremely large number of endemic species.

120997.q: What is a young endemic species called that has not yet been able to spread further since it arose?
120997.e: Neoendemics arose only a short time ago, for example on islands or in lakes. Their small range is a result of their young age.
120997.m: A neoendemic is a young species with a still narrow range.

120998.q: What is the opposite of an endemic species called, that is, a species found almost worldwide?
120998.e: Cosmopolitan species such as the housefly or bracken occur almost everywhere on Earth. Endemics, by contrast, are narrowly restricted.
120998.m: A cosmopolitan species is found almost all over the world.

a: An old species that now survives only in a remnant area
A young species that has only just arisen
An extinct species known as a fossil
A species newly introduced by humans
120999.e: Palaeoendemics used to be more widespread and have survived only in a refuge.
120999.m: Palaeoendemics are remnants of species that used to be more widespread.

121000.q: Why are there particularly many endemic species on remote islands?
a: The climate on islands is always tropical
Islands have no predators and no diseases
Endemic species are deliberately released on islands
121000.e: A few species that arrived continue to evolve without gene exchange with the mainland. This produces new species found only there, such as Darwin’s finches on the Galápagos Islands.
121000.m: Isolation promotes the formation of endemic species.

121001.q: Which seal species is endemic to a freshwater lake in Siberia?
121001.e: The Baikal seal lives only in Lake Baikal and is one of the few freshwater seals. The lake is home to many other endemic species.
121001.m: The Baikal seal occurs only in Lake Baikal.

121002.q: Which group of fish has produced many endemic species in Swiss lakes?
121002.e: In the Swiss lakes north of the Alps, numerous whitefish species arose after the last ice age, often living in just one lake. Some of them disappeared when many lakes were over-fertilised in the 20th century.
121002.m: Many endemic whitefish species live in Swiss lakes.

121003.q: Why are endemic species particularly threatened with extinction?
a: Their small range can be lost through a single disturbance
They basically only reproduce once in their lives
They are always very large animals
121003.e: If a species lives only on one island or in one lake, a single event such as an introduced predator can wipe out the whole population. That is why many endemic species are on the Red List.
121003.m: A small range makes endemic species vulnerable.

121004.q: Which flightless parrot is endemic to New Zealand and severely endangered?
121004.e: The kakapo lives only in New Zealand, is nocturnal and cannot fly. Introduced predators such as rats and stoats brought it to the brink of extinction.
121004.m: The flightless kakapo is endemic to New Zealand.

121005.q: Which federal office runs Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland (BDM)?
121005.e: The BDM is a programme of the FOEN. It provides long-term data on the development of biodiversity in Switzerland.
121005.m: Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland is a programme of the FOEN.

121006.q: Since which year has Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland been collecting data in the field?
121006.e: Field surveys of vascular plants and breeding birds began in 2001. Since then, the areas have been surveyed again at regular intervals.
121006.m: The BDM has been collecting biodiversity data since 2001.

121007.q: Why does Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland survey the same areas again and again at regular intervals?
a: To detect changes in biodiversity over time
Because new areas would be too expensive to buy
So that the animals get used to the researchers
Because rare species only live there
121007.e: Only repeated surveys at the same place show whether species are increasing or decreasing. This produces long data series on the development of biodiversity.
121007.m: Repeated surveys at the same place show trends in biodiversity.

121008.q: Which three groups of species does the BDM record in the landscape indicator Z7?
121008.e: On the 1 km² areas, vascular plants, butterflies and breeding birds are counted. These groups are well known and react to changes in the landscape.
121008.m: In the landscape indicator, the BDM counts plants, butterflies and breeding birds.

121009.q: Why are plants, mosses and snails particularly suitable for the small survey areas of biodiversity monitoring?
a: They stay in one place or hardly move
They are the only species in Switzerland
They only live on grid points
They are the easiest to catch and take away
121009.e: On a few square metres, it only makes sense to record living things that stay put. Birds or butterflies fly away and are therefore counted on larger areas.
121009.m: On small areas, mainly stationary organisms are recorded.

121010.q: Which groups of species does the BDM study on the 10 m² areas of indicator Z9?
121010.e: On the small areas, vascular plants, mosses and molluscs (snails) are identified. These groups stay in one place and are suitable for small areas.
121010.m: On small areas, the BDM records plants, mosses and snails.

121011.q: Why are the BDM sample areas on a regular grid rather than at selected places?
a: So that the results are representative of the whole of Switzerland
Because this makes them easier to reach on foot
Because species only live on grid points
So that as many rare species as possible are found
121011.e: A systematic sampling network prevents only especially beautiful or species-rich places from being studied. This way the BDM shows the average development, including in the ordinary landscape.
121011.m: A regular sampling network provides representative data.

121012.q: Which trend does the BDM show for the plant diversity of many Swiss habitats since 2001?
a: The species communities are becoming more similar (homogenisation)
The number of plant species has doubled
Rare specialists are increasing strongly everywhere
There are no changes at all
121012.e: The BDM shows that common species that like nutrients are spreading, while specialists are declining. As a result, the plant communities of different places are becoming alike.
121012.m: The homogenisation of species communities is a typical finding of the BDM.

121013.q: What is the official English abbreviation of the global biodiversity council?
121013.e: IPBES stands for Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services. The IPCC is its counterpart for the climate.
121013.m: The global biodiversity council is called IPBES in English.

121014.q: In which year was IPBES, the global biodiversity council, founded?
121014.e: IPBES was founded in April 2012 in Panama City by over 90 governments. It is meant to prepare scientific knowledge for policymakers.

121015.q: In which city is the secretariat of IPBES, the global biodiversity council, based?
121015.e: The IPBES secretariat is on the UN campus in Bonn. Other UN organisations dealing with the environment and climate are also based there.
121015.m: The secretariat of IPBES is in Bonn.

121016.q: What is meant by an invasive species?
a: An introduced species that spreads strongly and causes damage
A native species that is dying out
A species that only lives in zoos
A species that migrates away every year
121016.e: Invasive species were brought into new areas by humans. There they push out native species or cause damage. According to IPBES, they are among the five main drivers of biodiversity loss.
121016.m: Invasive species are introduced species that cause damage.

121017.q: Which direct driver of biodiversity loss ranks first in the 2019 IPBES report (on land and in fresh water)?
a: Changes in land and sea use
121017.e: IPBES names five drivers: change in use, direct exploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive species. For land and fresh water, change in use has the greatest influence.
121017.m: The conversion of habitats is the most important driver of species loss.

121018.q: Which other body is IPBES, the global biodiversity council, often compared with?
a: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)
121018.e: Like the IPCC, IPBES does not carry out its own research but summarises the state of knowledge in reports. These are approved by governments.
121018.m: IPBES is to biodiversity what the IPCC is to the climate.

121019.q: What was the topic of the first thematic assessment report by IPBES in 2016?
121019.e: The first thematic report dealt with pollinators such as bees and their importance for food. It showed that many crops depend on pollination.
121019.m: The first IPBES report was devoted to pollinators.

121020.q: What is the job of IPBES, the global biodiversity council?
a: To prepare scientific knowledge on biodiversity for political decisions
To pass binding laws on species protection
To manage nature reserves worldwide itself
To impose penalties on environmental offenders
121020.e: IPBES is an interface between science and politics. It assesses the state of knowledge but may not adopt binding rules.
121020.m: IPBES advises policymakers with scientific reports.

121021.q: Where and when was the Kunming-Montreal agreement adopted?
121021.e: The 15th Conference of the Parties (COP15) was chaired by China but took place in Montreal because of the pandemic. The global biodiversity framework was adopted on 19 December 2022.
121021.m: The Kunming-Montreal agreement was adopted in Montreal in December 2022.

121022.q: What does the best-known target of the Kunming-Montreal agreement, “30 by 30”, require?
a: Effectively protecting 30 per cent of land and sea areas by 2030
30 new national parks per country by 2030
121022.e: Target 3 requires at least 30 per cent of land, inland water and sea areas to be protected by 2030. When it was agreed, the figures worldwide were about 17 per cent on land and about 8 per cent at sea.
121022.m: The “30 by 30” target aims to protect thirty per cent of the Earth by 2030.

121023.q: Under which international convention was the Kunming-Montreal framework adopted?
a: Montreal Protocol on the ozone layer
121023.e: The framework was adopted at the 15th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, which was created in Rio in 1992. The Montreal Protocol of 1987, by contrast, concerns the ozone layer.
121023.m: The Kunming-Montreal agreement belongs to the Convention on Biological Diversity.

121024.q: According to the agreement, what proportion of damaged ecosystems is to be restored by 2030?
121024.e: Target 2 requires at least 30 per cent of degraded ecosystems to be effectively restored by 2030. This complements the protection target.
121024.m: Thirty per cent of damaged ecosystems are also to be restored.

121025.q: According to the Kunming-Montreal agreement, which subsidies are to be reduced?
121025.e: Target 18 requires incentives that harm nature, such as subsidies that encourage overuse, to be reduced. They are to fall by at least 500 billion dollars per year by 2030.
121025.m: Subsidies that harm nature are to be reduced.

121026.q: According to Kunming-Montreal, by how much should the overall risk from pesticides fall by 2030?
121026.e: Target 7 requires nutrient losses and the overall risk from pesticides and highly hazardous chemicals to be at least halved. A complete ban is not planned.
121026.m: The risk from pesticides is to be at least halved by 2030.

121027.q: What is the vision of the Kunming-Montreal framework for 2050?
121027.e: The vision “Living in harmony with nature” already comes from the Strategic Plan for 2011 to 2020. By 2050, biodiversity is to be valued, conserved and restored.
121027.m: The vision for 2050 is living in harmony with nature.

121028.q: What are invasive alien species, whose spread the Kunming-Montreal agreement aims to slow down?
a: Introduced species that spread strongly and push out native ones
Native species that have become rare
Migratory birds that fly south in winter
121028.e: Examples in Switzerland are Japanese knotweed and the Asian hornet. Target 6 requires their introduction to be at least halved by 2030.
121028.m: Invasive species are introduced and push out native species.

121029.q: What is the highest decision-making body of the Convention on Biological Diversity called?
121029.e: At the Conference of the Parties, all parties meet about every two years. Targets such as the Kunming-Montreal framework are adopted there.
121029.m: The Conference of the Parties is the most important body of the Convention on Biological Diversity.

121030.q: Which three main goals does the Convention on Biological Diversity pursue?
a: Conservation, sustainable use, fair sharing of benefits
A ban on hunting, fishing and clearing forests
Counting, naming and collecting all species
121030.e: The CBD aims to conserve diversity, use its components sustainably and share the benefits from genetic resources fairly. In this way it links protection and development.
121030.m: The Convention on Biological Diversity combines protection, use and fair sharing.

121031.q: When did the Convention on Biological Diversity come into force?
121031.e: The convention came into force on 29 December 1993, after enough states had ratified it. Switzerland ratified it in 1994.
121031.m: The Convention on Biological Diversity has been in force since 1993.

121032.q: Which large state has still not joined the Convention on Biological Diversity (as of 2025)?
121032.e: The USA signed the convention in 1993 but never ratified it. Almost all other states in the world are parties.
121032.m: The USA has never ratified the Convention on Biological Diversity.

121033.q: What does the Nagoya Protocol to the Convention on Biological Diversity regulate?
a: Access to genetic resources and fair sharing of the benefits
The safety of genetically modified organisms
121033.e: The Nagoya Protocol of 2010 regulates who may use genetic resources and how profits, for example from medicines, are shared. It came into force in 2014.
121033.m: The Nagoya Protocol regulates the fair sharing of benefits from genetic resources.

121034.q: How many parties does the Convention on Biological Diversity have (as of 2025)?
121034.e: The convention has 196 parties, including the European Union. This makes it almost universal.
121034.m: Almost all states in the world are parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity.

121035.q: What were the 20 biodiversity targets for 2020 adopted by the convention in 2010 called?
121035.e: The Aichi Targets were adopted at COP10 in Nagoya (Aichi Prefecture). By 2020, none of them had been fully met worldwide.
121035.m: The Aichi Targets were the biodiversity targets for 2020.

121036.q: What is meant by ecosystem services?
a: Benefits that people gain from ecosystems
The work of nature conservation organisations
The food chain in an ecosystem
121036.e: Ecosystem services are all the goods and services that nature provides for people, such as food, clean water or recreation. The term makes the value of nature visible.
121036.m: Ecosystem services are the services nature provides for people.

121037.q: Which four categories of ecosystem services did the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment of 2005 distinguish?
a: Provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting services
Plant, animal, mineral and climatic services
Local, regional, national and global services
Short-term, medium-term, long-term and eternal services
121037.e: The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment grouped the services by their function. Supporting services such as soil formation make all the others possible.
121037.m: Ecosystem services are divided into provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting services.

121038.q: Which category does the pollination of fruit trees by insects belong to?
121038.e: Pollination regulates natural processes on which the harvest depends. The fruit itself, by contrast, would be a provisioning service.
121038.m: Pollination is one of the regulating ecosystem services.

121039.q: Which ecosystem service does the protection forest in the Swiss Alps particularly provide?
a: Protection against avalanches, rockfall and debris flows
Producing drinking water from sea water
121039.e: Protection forests hold back snow and stones and so protect settlements and transport routes. In Switzerland, a large part of the forest is designated as protection forest.
121039.m: The protection forest protects people in the Alps from natural hazards.

121040.q: Which category does relaxing on a walk in the woods belong to?
121040.e: Cultural services are non-material benefits such as recreation, inspiration or spiritual values. Wood from the forest, by contrast, would be a provisioning service.
121040.m: Recreation in nature is a cultural ecosystem service.

121041.q: Why do people try to express ecosystem services in money?
a: To make their value visible in political and economic decisions
So that nature can be sold to companies
Because otherwise ecosystems provide no services
To calculate taxes for wild animals
121041.e: What has no price is often overlooked in decisions. Studies such as TEEB show what costs arise when nature is lost.
121041.m: Valuing it in money makes the value of nature visible.

121042.q: Which category does soil formation belong to?
121042.e: Supporting services are basic processes such as soil formation, photosynthesis and nutrient cycling. Without them, the other services would not exist.
121042.m: Soil formation is a supporting ecosystem service.

121043.q: Roughly how high is the annual value of all global ecosystem services estimated to be in studies?
a: As high as or higher than the entire world economic output
About as high as the budget of a Swiss municipality
About one per cent of world economic output
121043.e: A well-known study by Robert Costanza in 1997 arrived at about 33 trillion dollars per year. That was more than the world economic output at the time.
121043.m: Nature’s services are enormously valuable economically.

121044.q: How many major mass extinctions (the “Big Five”) does the Earth’s history know of before today’s?
121044.e: Palaeontology distinguishes five major mass extinctions. That is why people today speak of the sixth.
121044.m: There were five major mass extinctions before today’s.

121045.q: Which mass extinction was the largest in Earth’s history?
a: The extinction at the end of the Permian
The extinction at the end of the Cretaceous
The extinction at the end of the Triassic
The extinction at the end of the Ordovician
121045.e: About 252 million years ago, around 90 per cent or more of marine species died out. The main cause is thought to be intense volcanism in Siberia.
121045.m: The Permian-Triassic event was the largest mass extinction.

121046.q: How does today’s mass extinction differ from the five earlier ones?
a: It is mainly caused by humans
It is triggered by an asteroid
It is happening much more slowly
121046.e: Earlier mass extinctions had natural causes such as volcanism or impacts. Today the drivers are habitat destruction, overexploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive species.
121046.m: The sixth mass extinction is caused by humans.

121047.q: Which mass extinction about 445 million years ago was linked to an ice age and a falling sea level?
a: The extinction at the end of the Ordovician
The extinction at the end of the Permian
The extinction at the end of the Cretaceous
The extinction at the end of the Triassic
121047.e: At the end of the Ordovician, almost all animals lived in the sea. A glaciation made the sea level fall and destroyed many shallow-water habitats.
121047.m: The Ordovician ended with a mass extinction caused by an ice age.

121048.q: When did the last passenger pigeon die, once the most common bird species in North America?
121048.e: The female “Martha” died in Cincinnati Zoo in 1914. Mass hunting and forest clearance had wiped out billions of birds within a few decades.
121048.m: The passenger pigeon died out in 1914, although it once numbered billions.

121049.q: Which flightless bird from Mauritius died out in the 17th century and became a symbol of extinction?
121049.e: The dodo disappeared a few decades after sailors arrived, partly because of introduced rats, pigs and monkeys. The saying “dead as a dodo” recalls this.
121049.m: The dodo is the best-known symbol of extinction caused by humans.

121050.q: According to the usual definition, what proportion of species must disappear in a geologically short time for it to count as a mass extinction?
121050.e: Palaeontologists usually speak of a mass extinction when around 75 per cent of species disappear in a short geological time. We have not reached that point today, but the trend is heading that way.
121050.m: A mass extinction wipes out about three quarters of all species.

121051.q: Which driver is considered the main cause of today’s species extinction on land?
a: Changes in the Earth’s magnetic field
121051.e: Forests, wetlands and meadows are turned into fields, settlements and roads. As a result, many species lose their habitat.
121051.m: Habitat loss is the most important reason for today’s species extinction.

121052.q: Which majority would the biodiversity initiative, as a popular initiative, have needed to be accepted?
a: A majority of voters and a majority of cantons
121052.e: A popular initiative changes the Federal Constitution. This requires a majority of those voting and a majority of the cantons.
121052.m: A popular initiative needs a majority of both the people and the cantons.

121053.q: What was the result of the vote on the biodiversity initiative?
a: Rejected with about 63 per cent voting no
Accepted with about 54 per cent voting yes
Rejected with about 51 per cent voting no
Accepted by the people but not by the cantons
121053.e: The initiative was clearly rejected on 22 September 2024, with about 63 per cent voting no. A majority of the cantons also said no.
121053.m: The biodiversity initiative was clearly rejected in 2024.

121054.q: What was the official title of the biodiversity initiative?
a: “For the future of our nature and landscape”
“For clean drinking water and healthy food”
121054.e: The initiative wanted the constitution to protect biodiversity as well as landscapes and townscapes worth protecting more strongly. Its short name was the biodiversity initiative.
121054.m: The biodiversity initiative was officially called “For the future of our nature and landscape”.

121055.q: Which organisations were among the backers of the biodiversity initiative?
a: Pro Natura, BirdLife Switzerland and the Swiss Heritage Society
The Farmers’ Union, the Trade Association and Economiesuisse
Swiss Olympic, the Swiss Alpine Club and Switzerland Tourism
121055.e: The initiative was launched by nature and heritage conservation organisations, including Pro Natura, BirdLife Switzerland, the Swiss Foundation for Landscape Conservation and the Swiss Heritage Society. The Farmers’ Union campaigned against it.
121055.m: Nature and heritage conservation organisations launched the biodiversity initiative.

121056.q: Which of these cantons accepted the biodiversity initiative?
121056.e: In Basel-Stadt, about 58 per cent voted yes; apart from Basel-Stadt, only Geneva accepted it. In rural cantons, the rejection was particularly clear.
121056.m: Basel-Stadt said yes to the biodiversity initiative.

121057.q: What, among other things, did the biodiversity initiative want to anchor in the Federal Constitution?
a: More land and money for biodiversity
A duty to eat a vegetarian diet
121057.e: The Confederation and the cantons would have had to provide the land, money and tools needed to safeguard biodiversity. Opponents warned of restrictions on farming and energy production.
121057.m: The initiative demanded more land and money for nature.

121058.q: What position had parliament taken on the biodiversity initiative?
a: It recommended rejection without a counter-proposal
It put forward a direct counter-proposal
121058.e: The Federal Council had presented an indirect counter-proposal, but the Council of States rejected it. So the initiative went to the vote without a counter-proposal.
121058.m: The biodiversity initiative went to the vote without a counter-proposal.

121059.q: Which argument did opponents of the biodiversity initiative often put forward?
a: It would restrict farming and renewable energy
It would ban the building of new schools
121059.e: The Farmers’ Union and business associations feared less land for production and obstacles to hydropower and solar plants. Supporters considered action on species protection urgent.
121059.m: Opponents saw disadvantages for farming and energy production.

121060.q: What is the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) particularly known for?
a: The Red List of Threatened Species
121060.e: The IUCN, founded in 1948, assesses worldwide how threatened animal and plant species are. It publishes the result in the Red List.
121060.m: The IUCN publishes the Red List of Threatened Species.

121061.q: Which three IUCN categories together count as “threatened”?
121061.e: Critically endangered (CR), endangered (EN) and vulnerable (VU) make up the group of threatened species.
121061.m: Threatened species are classified as CR, EN or VU.

121062.q: What does the IUCN category “NE” mean?
121062.e: NE (Not Evaluated) means that a species has not yet been assessed against the criteria at all. This applies to the vast majority of species on Earth.
121062.m: NE means that a species has not yet been assessed.

121063.q: What does the IUCN category “DD” mean?
a: The data are not sufficient for a classification
121063.e: Data Deficient means that too little is known to assess the risk of extinction. It does not mean that the species is not threatened.
121063.m: DD means that data are lacking for a classification.

121064.q: What does the IUCN category “CR” mean?
121064.e: CR stands for Critically Endangered and is the highest level of threat before extinction. A species is placed there, for example, when its population shrinks very sharply in a short time.
121064.m: CR is the highest threat level on the Red List.

121065.q: Which extra category do regional Red Lists such as Switzerland’s use?
121065.e: Regional lists adopt the IUCN categories and add RE (Regionally Extinct). This describes a species that has disappeared from Switzerland but still lives elsewhere.
121065.m: RE describes a species that has died out only in one region.

121066.q: What does the IUCN category “EW” mean?
121066.e: EW stands for Extinct in the Wild. The species lives only in zoos, gardens or breeding stations, as the Przewalski’s horse once did.
121066.m: EW means that a species only lives in human care.

121067.q: What does the IUCN category “LC” mean?
121067.e: LC stands for Least Concern. Widespread and common species such as the blackbird are classified like this.
121067.m: LC means that a species is not threatened.

121068.q: Why is the list of threatened species called the “Red List”?
a: Red is a warning colour that stands for danger
It was printed in red because there was no paper
It lists only red animals and plants
It comes from the Red Army
121068.e: Red is a typical warning and signal colour. The Red List warns that species could disappear without protection.
121068.m: The Red List warns of the loss of species.

121069.q: Which hotspot is considered the most species-rich in the world?
121069.e: The tropical Andes are home to about 30,000 species of vascular plants, about half of them endemic. Large differences in altitude create a great many habitats there.
121069.m: The tropical Andes are the most species-rich hotspot on Earth.

121070.q: According to the decision of the biodiversity conference COP16 (2024), who should pay into the Cali Fund?
a: Companies that use genetic data from nature
121070.e: Companies, for example in the pharmaceutical or seed industries, that use genetic sequence data from nature are to pay in part of their profits. The money is to benefit conservation projects and indigenous communities.
121070.m: The Cali Fund is meant to share profits from genetic data with nature.

121071.q: How many million years ago did an asteroid impact end the age of the dinosaurs (except birds)?
121071.e: At the end of the Cretaceous about 66 million years ago, an asteroid struck at Chicxulub in Mexico. Around three quarters of all species disappeared.
121071.m: The Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction 66 million years ago ended the age of the great dinosaurs.

121169.q: What does a live vaccine contain?
a: Weakened germs that can still multiply
Only individual proteins of the germ
121169.e: Live vaccines contain germs that can still multiply but are weakened so much that they normally do not cause the disease. The body reacts much as it would to a real infection.
121169.m: A live vaccine contains weakened germs that can still multiply.

121170.q: What is the deliberate weakening of a germ for a live vaccine called?
121170.e: In attenuation, a germ loses its ability to cause disease, for example through many passages in cell cultures. Its ability to trigger an immune response is kept.
121170.m: Attenuated germs are weakened but still trigger an immune response.

121171.q: Which combination vaccine is made of live vaccines?
121171.e: The MMR vaccine contains weakened measles, mumps and rubella viruses. The vaccines against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough and hepatitis, by contrast, are inactivated vaccines.
121171.m: The MMR vaccination is a live vaccination.

121172.q: For which group of people are live vaccines generally not suitable?
a: People with a severe immune deficiency
People with a mild cold without fever
121172.e: With a severe immune deficiency, the weakened germ can multiply out of control and cause illness. That is why live vaccines are then usually not allowed; they are also not given during pregnancy.
121172.m: With a severe immune deficiency, live vaccines are avoided.

121173.q: What gap is recommended if two live vaccines are not given on the same day?
121173.e: Two live vaccines are given either at the same time or at least four weeks apart. Otherwise the reaction to the first vaccination could weaken the effect of the second.
121173.m: Two live vaccines are given together or four weeks apart.

121174.q: Which vaccine against tuberculosis is a live vaccine with weakened cattle tuberculosis bacteria?
121174.e: BCG stands for Bacillus Calmette-Guérin, a weakened strain of Mycobacterium bovis. In Switzerland, BCG vaccination is now only used in special situations.
121174.m: The BCG vaccine against tuberculosis is a live vaccine.

121175.q: Why are one or two doses of a live vaccine often enough for long protection?
a: The germs multiply and imitate a real infection
They contain especially much aluminium as a booster
They are injected directly into the bloodstream
They contain ready-made antibodies from donor blood
121175.e: Because the weakened germs multiply in the body, the immune response is strong and wide-ranging, including T cells. This often gives long-lasting protection.
121175.m: Live vaccines imitate an infection and often protect for a long time.

121176.q: Which scientist developed a vaccine against rabies with a weakened germ in 1885?
121176.e: Louis Pasteur weakened the rabies germ in dried spinal cord from rabbits. In 1885 he used it to successfully treat Joseph Meister, a boy who had been bitten.
121176.m: Louis Pasteur developed the rabies vaccine in 1885.

121177.q: What is the hallmark of an inactivated vaccine?
a: It contains no germs that can multiply
It only works through the mucous membranes
121177.e: Inactivated vaccines contain killed germs, parts of them or toxins made harmless. They cannot multiply in the body and therefore cannot cause the disease.
121177.m: An inactivated vaccine cannot multiply in the body.

121178.q: What is a toxoid, as used in the tetanus vaccine?
a: A bacterial toxin that has been made harmless
An artificial mRNA for the toxin
121178.e: In a toxoid, the toxin, such as tetanus toxin, is detoxified chemically, for example with formaldehyde. But it keeps its structure, so the body makes antibodies against it.
121178.m: A toxoid is a detoxified bacterial toxin that still creates immunity.

121179.q: Which of these vaccinations is a toxoid vaccination?
121179.e: In diphtheria it is not the bacterium itself but its toxin that makes you ill. That is why diphtheria toxoid is used for vaccination; measles, yellow fever and chickenpox are live vaccinations.

121180.q: Why do inactivated vaccines usually need several doses for the primary course?
a: Without multiplying, they trigger a weaker immune response
They are excreted from the body at once
They only contain antibodies without memory
They only work after a year
121180.e: Because the antigens do not multiply, the stimulus for the immune system is weaker. Several doses and later boosters build up stable protection.
121180.m: Inactivated vaccines usually need several doses.

121181.q: How is the hepatitis B vaccine made today?
a: By genetic engineering in yeast cells, as a surface protein
121181.e: The vaccine contains the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), which is produced by genetic engineering, usually in yeast cells. It contains no complete viruses and therefore cannot cause an infection.
121181.m: The hepatitis B vaccine contains a genetically engineered virus protein.

121182.q: What are inactivated vaccines called that contain only individual, purified parts of the germ?
121182.e: Subunit vaccines contain only selected antigens, such as surface proteins. This makes them well tolerated, but they often need adjuvants.
121182.m: Subunit vaccines contain only selected parts of a germ.

121183.q: Which advantage of inactivated vaccines is important for people with an immune deficiency?
a: They work without any side effects
They protect against all germs at once
121183.e: Because inactivated vaccines contain no germs that can multiply, they are safe even when the immune system is weakened. The protection may then be weaker, however.
121183.m: Inactivated vaccines are safe even with an immune deficiency.

121184.q: Against which tick-borne disease in Switzerland is an inactivated vaccine used?
121184.e: The TBE vaccine contains inactivated viruses. The Federal Office of Public Health recommends it in almost all of Switzerland because infected ticks are widespread.
121184.m: An inactivated vaccine protects against TBE.

121185.q: What gets into the body cells with an mRNA vaccine against Covid-19?
a: Building instructions for the spike protein
A piece of DNA that is built into the genome
121185.e: The mRNA contains the blueprint for the spike protein of the virus. The cells make this protein for a short time, and the immune system learns to recognise it.
121185.m: The mRNA delivers the blueprint for a virus protein.

121186.q: Where in the cell is the vaccine mRNA translated into protein?
a: At the ribosomes in the cytoplasm
In the cell nucleus at the DNA
121186.e: The mRNA stays in the cytoplasm and is read there by ribosomes. It does not get into the cell nucleus and does not change the DNA.
121186.m: Vaccine mRNA is read at ribosomes in the cytoplasm.

121187.q: What are lipid nanoparticles in mRNA vaccines for?
a: They protect the mRNA and bring it into the cells
They kill the viruses in the blood
They colour the injection site so it can be seen
121187.e: Free mRNA would be broken down quickly. Tiny fat shells, the lipid nanoparticles, protect it and merge with the cell membrane.
121187.m: Lipid nanoparticles package the delicate mRNA.

121188.q: What happens to the vaccine mRNA after a few days?
a: It is broken down by the cell
It is permanently built into the genome
121188.e: mRNA is a short-lived molecule and is broken down by the cell's own enzymes. What remains is the immune memory.
121188.m: Vaccine mRNA is broken down after a short time.

121189.q: Who received the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work that made mRNA vaccines possible?
121189.e: Karikó and Weissman discovered that modified nucleosides make mRNA cause less inflammation. This base modification was crucial for effective mRNA vaccines.
121189.m: Karikó and Weissman received the 2023 Nobel Prize for mRNA research.

121190.q: Why can mRNA vaccines be adapted to new virus variants relatively quickly?
a: You only have to change the building instructions in the mRNA
New viruses have to be grown in hens' eggs
The mRNA adapts itself in the body
You only have to increase the dose
121190.e: Once the genome of a new variant is known, the building instructions for its spike protein are written into the mRNA. Otherwise production stays the same.
121190.m: With mRNA vaccines, only the building instructions are swapped.

121191.q: In which year was the first mRNA vaccine against Covid-19 approved in Switzerland?
121191.e: The vaccine from Pfizer and BioNTech was approved in December 2020. It was the first Covid-19 vaccine approved in Switzerland.
121191.m: The first mRNA vaccine was approved in Switzerland in December 2020.

121192.q: What practical drawback did the first mRNA vaccines against Covid-19 have?
a: They had to be stored deep-frozen
They had to be injected into a vein
They were only approved for children
They could only be given as a tablet
121192.e: mRNA is unstable, so the vaccine from Pfizer and BioNTech, for example, at first had to be stored at around minus 70 degrees Celsius. This made distribution harder.
121192.m: Early mRNA vaccines needed very cold storage.

121193.q: From which Latin word does “adjuvant” come?
121193.e: “Adiuvare” means to help or support. The adjuvant helps the antigen to trigger a strong immune response.
121193.m: An adjuvant is a helper for the immune system.

121194.q: Which adjuvants have been used most often in vaccines for almost 100 years?
121194.e: Aluminium hydroxide and aluminium phosphate have been used since the 1920s and 1930s, for example in tetanus and diphtheria vaccines. The amount per dose is very small.
121194.m: Aluminium salts are the oldest and most common adjuvants.

121195.q: Which type of vaccine usually needs no adjuvant?
121195.e: Live vaccines already trigger a strong immune response because the germs multiply. Inactivated vaccines, especially subunit and toxoid vaccines, on the other hand often need adjuvants.
121195.m: Live vaccines usually manage without an adjuvant.

121196.q: Which advantage of an adjuvant is important when vaccines are scarce, for example in a flu pandemic?
a: Less antigen is needed per dose
The vaccine is cheaper to transport
121196.e: With an adjuvant, a smaller amount of antigen is often enough for the same protection. In this way more doses can be made from the same production.

121197.q: Why is an adjuvant added to a vaccine?
121197.e: An adjuvant is an enhancer. It makes the immune system react more strongly to the antigen.
121197.m: An adjuvant strengthens the effect of a vaccination.

121198.q: Which side effect occurs more often with adjuvanted vaccines?
a: Redness and pain at the injection site
Loss of the sense of taste
121198.e: Because adjuvants stimulate a local inflammatory reaction, pain, redness or swelling at the injection site happen more often. These reactions usually fade after a few days.
121198.m: Adjuvants can irritate the injection site more.

121199.q: Which part of the vaccine is the antigen against which the body forms its defence?
121199.e: The antigen is a part of the germ or the weakened germ itself. The immune system learns to recognise it; the adjuvant only strengthens this reaction.
121199.m: The body forms its defence against the antigen.

121200.q: Why does a booster vaccination work faster and more strongly than the first vaccination?
a: The vaccine is twice as strong
The immune system is older by then
121200.e: After the primary course, memory B cells and memory T cells remain. At the booster they multiply quickly, and a strong secondary response develops.
121200.m: A booster wakes up the immune memory.

121201.q: Which antibody class dominates in the secondary response after a booster?
121201.e: In the first response, mainly IgM antibodies are made at first. In the secondary response, IgG antibodies with high binding strength dominate.

121202.q: What is the process called in which antibodies bind better and better after repeated contact with the antigen?
121202.e: In the germinal centres of the lymph nodes, B cells with especially well-binding antibodies are selected. As a result, the affinity of the antibodies rises after each booster.
121202.m: Through affinity maturation, antibodies bind better and better.

121203.q: At what intervals is the tetanus booster recommended in Switzerland for adults between 25 and 65?
121203.e: The Swiss vaccination schedule provides boosters at 25, 45 and 65. From 65, a booster is given every 10 years, as the immune response becomes weaker in old age.
121203.m: In Switzerland, adults up to 65 have a tetanus booster every 20 years.

121204.q: How often is a booster against TBE recommended in Switzerland?
121204.e: After the primary course of three doses, the TBE vaccination in Switzerland is boosted every 10 years. This applies to people who spend time in risk areas.
121204.m: The TBE vaccination is boosted every 10 years.

121205.q: Why is the flu vaccination given anew every year?
a: Flu viruses keep changing their surface proteins
The vaccine only works for one month
The memory cells die every winter
121205.e: Through antigenic drift, the haemagglutinin and neuraminidase of flu viruses constantly change. That is why the vaccine is adapted every year to the virus strains expected.
121205.m: Flu vaccines are adapted every year because of antigenic drift.

121206.q: What is the gradual fading of vaccine protection over time called?
121206.e: With some vaccinations, the antibody level drops over time and protection fades. Boosters make up for this effect.
121206.m: Fading vaccine protection is called waning immunity.

121207.q: What is the series of vaccinations called that builds up the first protection before later boosters?
121207.e: The primary course usually consists of several doses weeks or months apart. Only on top of this does the booster extend protection for years.
121207.m: The primary course comes before the booster.

121208.q: What does the basic reproduction number R0 tell you?
a: How many people one infected person infects on average when everyone is susceptible
How many people die of a disease
How long the incubation period lasts
How many people are already vaccinated
121208.e: R0 describes the average number of further infections caused by one case in a completely unprotected population. If R0 is greater than 1, a disease can spread.
121208.m: R0 counts infections per case in an unprotected population.

121209.q: A disease has an R0 of 4. What share of the population must at least be immune so that it no longer spreads?
121209.e: The threshold for herd immunity is 1 minus 1/R0. With R0 equal to 4, this gives 1 minus 0.25, which is 0.75, so 75 %.
121209.m: The herd immunity threshold is 1 minus 1 divided by R0.

121210.q: Which disease has one of the highest basic reproduction numbers, with an R0 of about 12 to 18?
121210.e: Measles is extremely contagious and spreads through the air. That is why herd protection needs a very high share of immune people.
121210.m: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases of all.

121211.q: Why does tetanus not have a meaningful basic reproduction number?
a: Tetanus is not passed from person to person
Tetanus is only spread by mosquitoes
121211.e: Tetanus spores get into wounds from the environment, for example from soil. As no person infects another, there is no herd immunity; everyone has to protect themselves by vaccination.
121211.m: Only your own vaccination protects you against tetanus.

121212.q: How is the effective reproduction number R related to R0 when a share s of the population is still susceptible?
a: R equals R0 divided by s
121212.e: The fewer people are still susceptible, the fewer infections succeed. With R0 equal to 3 and s equal to 0.5, R becomes 1.5.
121212.m: The effective reproduction number is R0 times the share of susceptible people.

121213.q: An infection has an R0 of 3. Without countermeasures, how many new infections arise from a single case in the fourth generation of infection?
121213.e: Each generation triples the number: 3, 9, 27, 81. In the fourth generation, there are therefore 3 to the power of 4, which is 81 new cases.
121213.m: If R0 is greater than 1, case numbers grow exponentially.

121214.q: Which value of the effective reproduction number means that an epidemic is dying down?
121214.e: If each case infects fewer than one other person on average, the number of new infections falls from generation to generation. At exactly 1, it stays roughly constant.
121214.m: An epidemic dies down when R is below 1.

121215.q: Which three quantities determine R0 in a simple model?
a: Contact rate, probability of transmission and length of infectiousness
Vaccination rate, death rate and age
121215.e: R0 is roughly the product of the number of contacts per day, the probability of infection per contact and the number of infectious days. Measures such as keeping a distance or isolation reduce these factors.
121215.m: R0 depends on contacts, transmission and how long someone is infectious.

121216.q: A disease has an R0 of 5 and the vaccine protects 90 % of those vaccinated. Roughly what vaccination rate is needed for herd protection?
121216.e: The threshold is 1 minus 1/5, which is 0.8. Because only 90 % of those vaccinated are protected, you need 0.8 divided by 0.9, which is around 0.89 or 89 %.
121216.m: If a vaccine is not fully effective, a higher vaccination rate is needed.

121217.q: What does the vaccination coverage rate describe?
a: The share of a population group that has received a certain vaccination
The number of vaccine doses made per year
How effective a vaccine is in the laboratory
The number of vaccination centres per canton
121217.e: The vaccination coverage rate shows what percentage of a group is vaccinated. It is often recorded separately by age and vaccine dose.
121217.m: The vaccination coverage rate is the share of vaccinated people in a group.

121218.q: At a school, 552 of 600 young people have had two doses of measles vaccine. What is the vaccination coverage rate?
121218.e: 552 divided by 600 gives 0.92. The vaccination coverage rate is therefore 92 %.
121218.m: The coverage rate is calculated as vaccinated people divided by the total number.

121219.q: What two-dose vaccination coverage rate does the WHO recommend to eliminate measles?
121219.e: Because measles is so contagious, at least 95 % of people need to be immune. Only then can chains of infection be reliably broken.

121220.q: In which age groups does Switzerland regularly record vaccination coverage in the cantons?
121220.e: The Swiss vaccination coverage monitoring checks the vaccination records of 2-, 8- and 16-year-olds. The data are published by the Federal Office of Public Health.
121220.m: In Switzerland, vaccination coverage is recorded for 2-, 8- and 16-year-olds.

121221.q: Why does a high vaccination coverage rate also protect people who cannot be vaccinated?
a: Because germs can hardly form chains of infection any more
Because vaccinated people breathe out antibodies
Because unvaccinated people then have fewer contacts
121221.e: If almost everyone is immune, a germ rarely meets susceptible people. In this way babies or people with weak immune systems are protected indirectly; this is called herd protection.
121221.m: High vaccination coverage also protects unvaccinated people indirectly.

121222.q: Why can measles outbreaks happen despite a high national vaccination coverage rate?
a: Unvaccinated people are often clustered in certain groups or regions
The measles vaccine only protects for one year
Measles is only spread by vaccinated people
Measles viruses only survive in cities
121222.e: Averages hide local gaps in vaccination. Where unvaccinated people cluster, for example in certain communities, the virus can spread.
121222.m: Local vaccination gaps allow outbreaks despite good averages.

121223.q: In a municipality, 85 % of children are vaccinated, and the vaccine works in 95 % of those vaccinated. What share of the children is protected as a result?
121223.e: Protected are 0.85 times 0.95, which is 0.8075. That is around 81 % of all children.
121223.m: Only the share of vaccinated people with an effective immune response is protected.

121224.q: What does the vaccination record show when vaccination coverage is surveyed?
a: Which vaccinations are documented and with how many doses
How high the current antibody level is
Which diseases the child has already had
What blood group the child has
121224.e: The surveys analyse the entries in the vaccination record. They count the documented vaccinations and doses, not measured antibodies.
121224.m: Vaccination coverage rates are based on documented vaccinations.

121225.q: From what age does the Swiss vaccination schedule recommend the yearly flu vaccination to everyone as a risk group?
121225.e: Older people have a much higher risk of severe flu and complications. That is why the flu vaccination is recommended to them every autumn.
121225.m: From 65, the flu vaccination is recommended every year.

121226.q: In the Swiss vaccination schedule, what are the vaccinations called that are recommended for everyone to protect personal and public health?
121226.e: The schedule distinguishes between basic vaccinations, supplementary vaccinations and vaccinations for risk groups. Basic vaccinations are recommended for the whole population, for example against measles or tetanus.
121226.m: Basic vaccinations are recommended for everyone.

121227.q: Against which three diseases does the MMR vaccination protect, which the Swiss vaccination schedule recommends for young children?
121227.e: MMR stands for measles, mumps and rubella. The schedule recommends two doses in early childhood so that reliable protection exists as early as possible.
121227.m: The MMR vaccination protects against measles, mumps and rubella.

121228.q: Apart from diphtheria, tetanus and whooping cough, against which diseases does the six-in-one vaccination for babies protect?
a: Polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b and hepatitis B
121228.e: The hexavalent vaccine protects against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, Hib and hepatitis B. It is given several times in the first year of life.
121228.m: The six-in-one vaccination also covers polio, Hib and hepatitis B.

121229.q: Why does the Swiss vaccination schedule recommend vaccinating babies in their first months of life?
a: Diseases such as whooping cough are especially dangerous for babies
Babies tolerate vaccinations better than adults
Later on vaccinations no longer work at all
Babies are protected against everything from birth
121229.e: Some infections, such as whooping cough, are particularly severe in babies and can be life-threatening. That is why protection should be built up as early as possible.
121229.m: Early vaccinations protect babies from dangerous diseases.

121230.q: At what age does the Swiss vaccination schedule recommend the hepatitis B vaccination if it was not given in infancy?
121230.e: The hepatitis B vaccination is preferably given in infancy. If it is missing, it should be caught up in young people between 11 and 15.
121230.m: Young people catch up on a missing hepatitis B vaccination at 11 to 15.

121231.q: Is there a general duty to be vaccinated in Switzerland?
a: No, vaccinations are voluntary in principle
Yes, but only in French-speaking Switzerland
Yes, for all children before kindergarten
121231.e: Vaccinations are voluntary in Switzerland. The law only allows the cantons, in exceptional cases, to make a vaccination compulsory for groups at risk or certain jobs.
121231.m: In Switzerland, vaccinations are voluntary in principle.

121232.q: In the Swiss vaccination schedule, what are vaccinations called that offer individual protection but are not counted as basic for everyone?
121232.e: Supplementary vaccinations mainly protect the vaccinated person against particular risks. Doctors give information about them, and the decision is an individual one.
121232.m: Supplementary vaccinations offer extra personal protection.

121233.q: What kind of body is the EKIF, the Federal Commission for Vaccination?
a: An extra-parliamentary commission of the Confederation
A commission of the National Council
A private foundation of the pharmaceutical industry
121233.e: Extra-parliamentary commissions advise the Federal Council and the administration with outside expertise. The EKIF is such a commission for all questions about vaccinations.
121233.m: The EKIF is an extra-parliamentary commission of the Confederation.

121234.q: What is the main job of the EKIF?
a: It draws up vaccination recommendations and advises the FOPH and the Federal Council
It approves vaccines for the market
It produces vaccines for the army
It imposes fines for missing vaccinations
121234.e: The EKIF assesses scientific data and draws up vaccination recommendations together with the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH). Approving vaccines, by contrast, is the job of another federal authority.
121234.m: The EKIF draws up vaccination recommendations.

121235.q: Which authority, not the EKIF, is responsible for approving vaccines in Switzerland?
a: The Swiss Academies of Arts and Sciences
The Federal Office for the Environment
121235.e: Swissmedic checks quality, safety and effectiveness and grants approval. Only afterwards does the EKIF decide whether and for whom a vaccination is recommended.

121236.q: Who chooses the members of the EKIF?
121236.e: The EKIF is set up by the Federal Council. Its members are experts from medicine and healthcare.
121236.m: The Federal Council chooses the members of the EKIF.

121237.q: What is the German counterpart of the EKIF, based at the Robert Koch Institute, called?
121237.e: In Germany, STIKO publishes the vaccination recommendations. It has a similar role to the EKIF in Switzerland.

121238.q: What role do recommendations from the FOPH and the EKIF play in the cost of a vaccination in Switzerland?
a: Recommended vaccinations are usually paid for by basic health insurance
Recommended vaccinations always have to be paid for yourself
They have no influence on costs
121238.e: For many recommended vaccinations, compulsory health insurance covers the costs if they are listed in the health care benefits ordinance. Travel vaccinations are usually not covered.
121238.m: Recommended vaccinations are usually covered by basic health insurance.

121239.q: What kinds of data does the EKIF take into account for a new vaccination recommendation?
a: Burden of disease, effectiveness, safety and costs
Only the recommendations from the USA
121239.e: The commission weighs up how common and severe a disease is and how well and safely the vaccine works. Practicality and cost-effectiveness are also included.
121239.m: Vaccination recommendations are based on weighing up many data.

121240.q: Which organisation in the USA draws up vaccination recommendations in a similar way to the EKIF?
121240.e: ACIP advises the US health authority CDC on vaccination recommendations. The FDA approves vaccines, much like Swissmedic, and the NIH fund research.
121240.m: In the USA, ACIP recommends vaccinations and the FDA approves them.

121241.q: Roughly how high was the death rate for the severe form of smallpox, variola major?
121241.e: About one in three people who fell ill died of variola major. Many survivors were left with scars or went blind.
121241.m: The severe form of smallpox killed about one in three people who caught it.

121242.q: Who carried out the first vaccination with cowpox against smallpox in 1796?
121242.e: The English country doctor Edward Jenner vaccinated the boy James Phipps with material from cowpox. Afterwards the boy was protected against real smallpox.
121242.m: In 1796 Edward Jenner vaccinated with cowpox for the first time.

121243.q: Where does the word “vaccine” come from?
121243.e: The term recalls Jenner's vaccination with cowpox. “Vaccinia” was the name for cowpox.
121243.m: Vaccine comes from the Latin word for cow.

121244.q: What was the older method called in which people were inoculated with material from real smallpox pustules?
121244.e: In variolation, material from smallpox patients was put into small cuts in the skin. This usually led to milder illness, but it was risky and could infect others.
121244.m: Variolation used real smallpox germs and was dangerous.

121245.q: In which year did the World Health Organization officially declare smallpox eradicated?
121245.e: After the last natural case in Somalia in 1977, the World Health Assembly confirmed the eradication on 8 May 1980. It was the first human disease to be eradicated.
121245.m: Smallpox has been considered eradicated since 1980.

121246.q: Which strategy was decisive in the smallpox eradication programme?
a: Surveillance and ring vaccination around every case
Building smallpox hospitals in every town
121246.e: Instead of vaccinating everyone, each case was tracked down and the contacts around it were vaccinated in a targeted way. This strategy is called “surveillance and containment”.
121246.m: Smallpox was eradicated with surveillance and ring vaccination.

121247.q: Which feature of smallpox made its eradication possible?
a: The virus had no animal reservoir
The virus was not very contagious
The virus only lived in mosquitoes
121247.e: Smallpox only infected humans, and sick people were easy to recognise by the pustules. In addition, there was a stable, effective vaccine with long protection.
121247.m: Without an animal reservoir, the smallpox virus could be eradicated.

121248.q: Which simple instrument made vaccinating against smallpox much easier from the late 1960s?
a: The glass syringe with a plunger
121248.e: The bifurcated needle held a drop of vaccine between its two prongs. It was cheap, saved vaccine and could be learned quickly even by non-specialists.
121248.m: The bifurcated needle helped with smallpox vaccination worldwide.

121249.q: Which other infectious disease was eradicated after smallpox, though it is an animal disease?
121249.e: Rinderpest was declared eradicated in 2011 by the World Organisation for Animal Health and the FAO. It is so far the only animal disease to have been eradicated.

121250.q: Which cells does the poliovirus damage in polio?
a: Motor nerve cells in the spinal cord
121250.e: The poliovirus can destroy the motor nerve cells in the front horn of the spinal cord. The muscles they supply then stop working, and floppy paralysis results.
121250.m: Polio destroys motor nerve cells in the spinal cord.

121251.q: How is the poliovirus mainly transmitted?
a: Faecal-oral, through dirty hands, water or food
121251.e: Polioviruses are enteroviruses and multiply in the gut. They are shed in the stool and passed on through contaminated water or hands.

121252.q: Roughly what share of infections with polioviruses lead to paralysis?
121252.e: The great majority of infections cause no symptoms or only mild ones. Fewer than one per cent lead to paralysis, which is why the virus can spread unnoticed.

121253.q: Who developed the first successful inactivated polio vaccine, approved in 1955?
121253.e: Jonas Salk inactivated the polioviruses with formaldehyde. His vaccine (IPV) is injected and is also used in Switzerland today.
121253.m: Jonas Salk developed the injected inactivated polio vaccine.

121254.q: What risk does Sabin's oral live polio vaccine carry?
a: Rarely, disease-causing vaccine viruses can develop from it
It often causes allergies to sugar
It does not protect against polio at all
It has to be repeated every year
121254.e: The weakened vaccine viruses are shed and can change in poorly vaccinated populations. In this way, circulating vaccine-derived polioviruses rarely arise.
121254.m: The oral polio vaccine can rarely give rise to disease-causing vaccine viruses.

121255.q: In which two countries was wild polio still endemic in 2025?
121255.e: Thanks to the global polio initiative, the wild virus has almost disappeared. As of 2025, it is only endemic in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
121255.m: Wild polio is only endemic in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

121256.q: Which types of wild poliovirus are already considered eradicated?
121256.e: Wild poliovirus type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015 and type 3 in 2019. Only type 1 is still circulating.
121256.m: Only wild poliovirus type 1 is still circulating.

121257.q: Which device kept polio patients with paralysed breathing muscles alive in the 1950s?
121257.e: The iron lung creates low pressure in a closed tank so that the chest rises. In this way patients could breathe despite paralysed breathing muscles.
121257.m: The iron lung helped polio patients breathe using low pressure.

121258.q: When was the WHO European Region certified polio-free?
121258.e: The WHO European Region, which includes Switzerland, was declared free of wild polio in June 2002. But the virus can still be brought in, so vaccination continues.
121258.m: Europe has been certified polio-free since 2002.

121259.q: What is the aim of contact tracing?
a: Finding contacts of infected people and breaking chains of infection
Developing new vaccines in the laboratory
Counting the number of hospital beds
121259.e: In contact tracing, people who have had contact with an infected person are identified. They are informed, tested or sent into quarantine before they infect others.
121259.m: Contact tracing breaks chains of infection.

121260.q: What is the difference between isolation and quarantine?
a: Isolation is for sick people, quarantine for people who may have been infected
Isolation is for animals, quarantine for humans
Isolation always lasts longer than a year
121260.e: People who are confirmed to be infected stay in isolation. Quarantine concerns healthy contacts who could have been infected and are therefore kept apart as a precaution.
121260.m: Isolation is for the sick, quarantine for those who may have been infected.

121261.q: What is it called when tracers find out where an infected person caught the infection themselves?
121261.e: Backward tracing looks for the source of infection, such as an event. In this way superspreading events and further cases from the same source are found.
121261.m: Backward tracing looks for the source of an infection.

121262.q: What is the first known infected person in an outbreak called?
121262.e: The index case is the starting point of the investigation. Contacts are traced from there.
121262.m: The index case stands at the start of contact tracing.

121263.q: Who was mainly responsible for contact tracing in Switzerland during the Covid-19 pandemic?
121263.e: Carrying out disease control is largely the job of the cantons. The cantonal medical services organised the contact tracing.
121263.m: In Switzerland, the cantons organise contact tracing.

121264.q: Which technology did the SwissCovid app use to record encounters?
121264.e: The app exchanged anonymous keys with nearby devices via Bluetooth. No locations were stored, and the matching took place in a decentralised way on the phone.
121264.m: The SwissCovid app used Bluetooth instead of location data.

121265.q: Which universities played a leading role in developing the decentralised DP-3T protocol for the SwissCovid app?
a: University of Basel and University of Bern
University of Geneva and University of Fribourg
121265.e: DP-3T stands for Decentralized Privacy-Preserving Proximity Tracing. It was developed by an international team led by EPFL and ETH Zurich.
121265.m: The DP-3T protocol comes from EPFL and ETH Zurich.

121266.q: Why does infection before symptoms start make contact tracing harder?
a: Infected people infect others before they know they are ill
Tests do not work at all before symptoms
121266.e: With presymptomatic transmission, tracing often starts too late. That is why testing and informing quickly are crucial.
121266.m: Presymptomatic transmission makes contact tracing harder.

121267.q: For how long are contacts usually monitored in the case of Ebola?
121267.e: The incubation period of Ebola is up to 21 days. Anyone who develops no symptoms during this time is considered not infected.
121267.m: With Ebola, contacts are watched for 21 days.

121268.q: What is the law of refraction for passing from medium 1 into medium 2?
a: n1 · sin α = n2 · sin β
n1 · cos α = n2 · cos β
n1 / sin α = n2 / sin β
121268.e: The product of the refractive index and the sine of the angle to the normal stays the same across the boundary. From this you can work out the angle of refraction.
121268.m: In the law of refraction, the product of refractive index and sine of the angle stays the same.

121269.q: Light passes at 45° from air (n equals 1.00) into water (n equals 1.33). Roughly what is the angle of refraction?
121269.e: sin β equals sin 45° / 1.33 equals 0.707 / 1.33 equals 0.532. So β is about 32°.
121269.m: When light enters water, the angle to the normal gets smaller.

121270.q: Light passes at 50° from air into glass with n equal to 1.60. Roughly what is the angle of refraction?
121270.e: sin β equals sin 50° / 1.60 equals 0.766 / 1.60 equals 0.479. The arcsine of this is about 28.6°.
121270.m: The greater the refractive index, the more strongly light is bent towards the normal.

121271.q: A ray of light hits a plastic from air at 60° and travels inside it at 35° to the normal. Roughly what is the refractive index of the plastic?
121271.e: n equals sin 60° / sin 35° equals 0.866 / 0.574, about 1.51. Here n for air is taken as 1.
121271.m: The refractive index can be found from the angles of incidence and refraction.

121272.q: A ray in glass (n equals 1.50) meets the boundary with air at 25° to the normal. Roughly at what angle does it come out?
121272.e: sin β equals 1.50 · sin 25° equals 1.50 · 0.423 equals 0.634. So β is about 39.3°.
121272.m: When light passes out into air, the angle to the normal gets bigger.

121273.q: The law of refraction is named after which scientist, who found it around 1621?
121273.e: The Dutch mathematician Willebrord van Roijen Snell formulated the law around 1621. René Descartes published it independently in 1637.
121273.m: The law of refraction is named after Snell.

121274.q: From what are the angles of incidence and refraction measured in the law of refraction?
a: From the optical axis of a lens
121274.e: The angles are measured from the normal, the line at right angles to the boundary at the point where the ray hits. So a ray that just grazes the surface has almost 90°.
121274.m: In optics, angles are measured from the normal.

121275.q: Light passes at 40° from water (n equals 1.33) into glass (n equals 1.50). Roughly what is the angle of refraction?
121275.e: sin β equals 1.33 · sin 40° / 1.50 equals 1.33 · 0.643 / 1.50 equals 0.570. So β is about 34.7°.
121275.m: The law of refraction applies to any pair of media.

121276.q: Which principle explains the law of refraction as the path with the shortest travel time?
121276.e: According to Fermat, light between two points takes a path for which the travel time is extreme, usually minimal. Because light is slower in the denser medium, the path bends at the boundary.
121276.m: Light takes the path with the shortest travel time.

121277.q: How is the refractive index n of a medium defined?
a: Speed of light in a vacuum divided by speed of light in the medium
Density of the medium divided by density of water
Wavelength in the medium times frequency
Angle of incidence divided by angle of refraction
121277.e: n equals c / v. The slower light is in the medium, the greater the refractive index.
121277.m: The refractive index compares the speed of light in a vacuum with that in the medium.

121278.q: How fast is light in glass with n equal to 1.5?
121278.e: v equals c / n equals 3.0 · 10⁸ m/s / 1.5 equals 2.0 · 10⁸ m/s. So light in glass is a third slower.
121278.m: In glass, light is about a third slower than in a vacuum.

121279.q: Which substance has a refractive index of about 1.31, slightly less than liquid water?
121279.e: Frozen water has a lower density than liquid water and a refractive index of about 1.31. Diamond, flint glass and sapphire are much higher.
121279.m: Ice refracts light slightly less than liquid water.

121280.q: Why does the refractive index of air change slightly with the weather?
a: It depends on the air density, so on pressure and temperature
It depends on the wind direction
It depends on the time of day
It depends on the colour of the sky
121280.e: The denser a gas is, the more molecules interact with the light and the greater the refractive index. Warm air has a lower density and refracts light slightly less.
121280.m: The refractive index of gases depends on their density.

121281.q: What is the refractive index of a vacuum?
121281.e: In a vacuum the speed of light is c, so n equals c / c equals 1. For visible light, practically all substances have a refractive index greater than 1.
121281.m: A vacuum has a refractive index of 1.

121282.q: Roughly what is the refractive index of air under normal conditions?
121282.e: Air refracts light only very slightly; its refractive index is about 1.0003. So in many calculations it is taken as 1.
