121597.e: Penicillin G is sensitive to acid and would be largely broken down in the stomach. Penicillin V is more stable in acid and can be taken as a tablet.

121598.q: Which unwanted reaction to penicillin is the best known?
121598.e: Penicillin allergies are among the most common drug allergies and range from skin rashes to anaphylactic shock. Discoloured teeth, by contrast, are typical of tetracyclines.

121599.q: What do staphylococci typically look like under the microscope?
a: Spheres in clusters like bunches of grapes
121599.e: Staphylé is the Greek word for a bunch of grapes. Spherical bacteria in chains, by contrast, are streptococci.
121599.m: Staphylococci lie together like bunches of grapes.

121600.q: Where does Staphylococcus aureus live in many healthy people without making them ill?
121600.e: Around 20 to 30 per cent of people carry Staphylococcus aureus in their nose, some of them permanently. It only becomes dangerous when it gets into the body, for example through wounds.
121600.m: Many healthy people carry staphylococci in their nose.

121601.q: Which measure is most important in hospital to prevent MRSA from being passed on?
a: Taking the temperature of all visitors
121601.e: MRSA is mainly carried from patient to patient on the hands of staff. Hand disinfection breaks this route most effectively.
121601.m: Hand disinfection stops MRSA from spreading.

121602.q: What does the “R” in the abbreviation MRSA stand for?
121602.e: MRSA means methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. These bacteria are not affected by methicillin and related antibiotics such as penicillins.
121602.m: MRSA is resistant to methicillin and related antibiotics.

121603.q: Why are MRSA infections harder to treat than ordinary staphylococcal infections?
a: Many common antibiotics no longer work
121603.e: The usual beta-lactam antibiotics fail against MRSA. Doctors have to switch to a few reserve drugs such as vancomycin, which can have more side effects.
121603.m: Many common antibiotics do not work against MRSA.

121604.q: What does decolonisation mean for MRSA carriers?
a: The bacteria are removed from the skin and mucous membranes
The person is moved to another country
The bacteria are grown in the laboratory
The person is given a vaccine against MRSA
121604.e: Nasal ointments and antiseptic washes, for example, are used for several days. The aim is that the person no longer carries the bacteria and passes them on.

121605.q: In which decade was MRSA first described, shortly after methicillin was introduced?
121605.e: Methicillin came onto the market in 1959, and resistant strains were already described in Great Britain in 1961. This shows how quickly bacteria adapt.
121605.m: MRSA appeared as early as the 1960s.

121606.e: Prions contain no genetic material but are proteins with an abnormal three-dimensional folding. This makes them fundamentally different from viruses and bacteria.
121606.m: Prions are disease-causing proteins without genetic material.

121607.q: Who coined the term prion and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for it in 1997?
121607.e: In 1982 the American Stanley Prusiner described prions as protein-like infectious particles. His theory was controversial for a long time.

121608.q: Which animal disease, which also concerned Switzerland in the 1990s, is caused by prions?
121608.e: Bovine spongiform encephalopathy, known as mad cow disease, also occurred in Swiss cattle. The other diseases are caused by viruses.
121608.m: BSE is a prion disease of cattle.

121609.q: Which human disease is caused by prions?
121609.e: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease quickly destroys nerve tissue in the brain and is fatal. One variant has been linked to eating beef contaminated with BSE.
121609.m: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a prion disease.

121610.q: How do prions multiply in the body?
a: They make normal proteins fold wrongly too
They build their genetic material into the DNA
They form spores in the nerve cells
121610.e: A misfolded prion protein acts like a template and changes the shape of healthy proteins. This creates a chain reaction, and the faulty proteins build up as deposits.
121610.m: Prions multiply by refolding healthy proteins.

121611.q: Why do surgical instruments need special treatment if prions are suspected?
a: Prions survive many usual sterilisation methods
121611.e: Prions are very resistant to heat, radiation and many disinfectants. That is why especially strict cleaning rules apply to them.

121612.q: What is the prion disease of sheep and goats called?
121612.e: Scrapie has been known since the 18th century; sick animals often rub themselves against fences. Distemper, foot rot and mange have other causes.
121612.m: Scrapie is the prion disease of sheep.

121613.q: In which country did the prion disease kuru occur?
121613.e: Kuru affected the Fore people in the highlands of Papua New Guinea. It was passed on through ritual funeral customs and disappeared after these were given up.
121613.m: Kuru was a prion disease in Papua New Guinea.

121614.q: Which enzyme in retroviruses copies RNA into DNA?
121614.e: Reverse transcriptase reverses the usual flow of information from DNA to RNA. This is also where the name retrovirus comes from.
121614.m: Retroviruses copy their RNA into DNA.

121615.q: Which is the best-known retrovirus that makes humans ill?
121615.e: The human immunodeficiency virus is a retrovirus and, if untreated, can lead to the disease AIDS. Flu, measles and hepatitis A viruses are not retroviruses.
121615.m: HIV is one of the retroviruses.

121616.q: Which immune cells does HIV mainly attack?
121616.e: HIV docks onto the surface protein CD4, which is carried mainly by T helper cells. If these cells fail, the whole immune defence is weakened.
121616.m: HIV mainly destroys T helper cells.

121617.q: What is the DNA of a retrovirus called once it is built into the host cell's genome?
121617.e: The provirus stays permanently in the cell's genome and is copied with every division. That is why an HIV infection cannot yet be cured completely.
121617.m: Built-in retrovirus DNA is called a provirus.

121618.q: Which enzyme of a retrovirus builds the newly made viral DNA into the host genome?
121618.e: Integrase cuts open the host DNA and inserts the viral DNA. Integrase inhibitors are an important part of HIV treatment today.
121618.m: Integrase builds viral DNA into the genome.

121619.q: Why was the discovery of reverse transcriptase around 1970 so important?
a: It showed that genetic information can also flow from RNA to DNA
It showed that viruses have no genetic information
It proved that DNA is made of proteins
It led directly to a cure for AIDS
121619.e: People had assumed that information only flows from DNA to RNA. But retroviruses copy their RNA into DNA. The discoverers received the Nobel Prize in 1975.
121619.m: Retroviruses reverse the flow of information.

121620.q: What kind of genetic material do retroviruses carry in the virus particle?
121620.e: Each retrovirus particle contains two copies of single-stranded RNA. Only in the host cell is it turned into double-stranded DNA.
121620.m: Retroviruses carry their genetic material as RNA.

121621.q: What are endogenous retroviruses in the human genome?
a: Remains of old virus infections passed down for generations
Active viruses that make every person ill
Bacteria living in the cell nucleus
Genes that only appear during illness
121621.e: Millions of years ago, retroviruses built their DNA into the germ cells of our ancestors. These traces have been inherited ever since and are mostly inactive.
121621.m: Our genome contains many remains of old retroviruses.

121622.q: What is typical of a parasite?
a: It lives at the expense of a host
It lives only on dead material
121622.e: A parasite takes nutrients from its host and harms it, but usually does not kill it straight away. When both partners benefit, it is called symbiosis.
121622.m: A parasite lives at the expense of its host.

121623.q: Which of these organisms is an ectoparasite?
121623.e: Ectoparasites live on the outside of the host's body, like the tick on the skin. Tapeworm, roundworm and liver fluke live inside the body and are endoparasites.
121623.m: Ectoparasites live on the outside of their host.

121624.q: What is the host called in which a parasite reaches its adult stage?
121624.e: In the definitive host, the parasite becomes adult and reproduces. Only larval or young stages live in the intermediate host.
121624.m: A parasite becomes adult in the definitive host.

121625.q: Which animals are the typical intermediate hosts of the fox tapeworm?
121625.e: Mice take in the worm eggs, and larvae grow in their liver. When a fox eats the mouse, the cycle is complete; humans can be infected as accidental hosts.
121625.m: Mice are the intermediate hosts of the fox tapeworm.

121626.q: What is a relationship called in which one partner benefits and the other neither benefits nor is harmed?
121626.e: In commensalism, an animal might for example use another's food scraps without harming it. In parasitism, by contrast, the host is harmed.
121626.m: Commensals help themselves without harming their partner.

121627.q: Which native bird is a well-known brood parasite?
121627.e: The female cuckoo lays her eggs in other birds' nests. The host birds raise the cuckoo chick, often at the expense of their own young.
121627.m: The cuckoo has its young raised by other birds.

121628.q: Which bacterial disease is most often passed on by ticks in Switzerland?
121628.e: Lyme disease is caused by bacteria of the genus Borrelia and can be treated with antibiotics. There is a vaccine against TBE, which is also passed on by ticks but is caused by a virus.
121628.m: In Switzerland, ticks mainly pass on Lyme disease.

121629.q: Which animal is the definitive host of the parasite Toxoplasma gondii?
121629.e: Only in cats and other felines can Toxoplasma complete its full life cycle. Mice and also humans are intermediate hosts.
121629.m: Cats are the definitive hosts of Toxoplasma.

121630.q: Which mosquitoes pass the malaria parasites on to humans?
121630.e: Only females of the genus Anopheles pass on plasmodia when they suck blood. The tiger mosquito passes on other diseases, such as dengue.
121630.m: Malaria is spread by Anopheles mosquitoes.

121631.q: To which group of disease-causing organisms do plasmodia belong?
121631.e: Plasmodia are single-celled organisms with a nucleus, in other words eukaryotes. That is why antibiotics against bacteria do not help against malaria.
121631.m: Malaria is caused by single-celled organisms.

121632.q: Which species of Plasmodium causes the most dangerous form of malaria?
121632.e: Plasmodium falciparum causes falciparum malaria, which is often fatal if untreated. Infected blood cells stick together in small vessels, for example in the brain.
121632.m: Plasmodium falciparum is the most dangerous malaria parasite.

121633.q: Which blood cells do plasmodia attack in the human body?
121633.e: The parasites multiply in the red blood cells and make them burst. Many cells bursting at the same time leads to bouts of fever.
121633.m: Plasmodia multiply in red blood cells.

121634.q: Which organ do plasmodia travel to first after a mosquito bite?
121634.e: The parasites first multiply unnoticed in liver cells. Only after that do they get into the blood and cause the signs of illness.
121634.m: Plasmodia first multiply in the liver.

121635.q: For discovering which malaria drug did the Chinese researcher Tu Youyou receive the Nobel Prize in 2015?
121635.e: Tu Youyou obtained artemisinin from sweet wormwood, a plant used in traditional Chinese medicine. Combination therapies with artemisinin are standard today against falciparum malaria.
121635.m: Artemisinin is an important malaria drug from a plant.

121636.q: Which inherited blood disease, in its mild form with only one copy of the gene, partly protects against malaria?
121636.e: Carriers with one copy of the sickle cell gene are less likely to become seriously ill with falciparum malaria. That is why the gene is common in the malaria regions of Africa.
121636.m: The sickle cell gene gives some protection against malaria.

121637.q: What best protects travellers in malaria regions from infection?
a: Protection against mosquitoes and, depending on the region, preventive medicines
Having no contact with sick people
A single vaccination before the trip
121637.e: Malaria is spread by mosquito bites, not by water or direct contact. Mosquito nets, long clothing and insect repellent help, and in some regions tablets as well.
121637.m: Protection against mosquitoes is the main defence against malaria.

a: An infection caught in hospital or a care home
An infection that only affects animals
121638.e: Nosocomial comes from the Greek nosokomeion, hospital. It means infections that arise in connection with a stay or treatment in a healthcare facility.

121639.q: From when after admission to hospital is an infection usually considered nosocomial?
a: At the earliest about 48 hours after admission
121639.e: If an infection only appears after about 48 hours and was not present or incubating on admission, it is put down to the hospital. Earlier infections were usually brought in from home.
121639.m: After about 48 hours in hospital, a new infection counts as nosocomial.

121640.q: Which doctor reduced childbed fever in Vienna in 1847 through handwashing with chlorinated lime?
121640.e: Semmelweis realised that doctors were carrying disease material from corpses to patients. With a chlorinated lime solution, the death rate on his ward fell sharply.
121640.m: Ignaz Semmelweis is considered a pioneer of hand hygiene.

121641.q: Which medical device especially increases the risk of a urinary tract infection in hospital?
121641.e: Bacteria can get directly into the bladder through the catheter tube. That is why a urinary catheter should only stay in for as long as necessary.
121641.m: Urinary catheters encourage urinary tract infections.

121642.q: What is the Swiss national centre for infection prevention called, which records hospital infections?
121642.e: Swissnoso carries out surveillance of wound infections after operations and runs infection prevention programmes. Swissmedic, by contrast, is the authority for medicines.
121642.m: Swissnoso deals with hospital infections in Switzerland.

121643.q: According to the WHO, for how long should hands be rubbed with an alcohol-based disinfectant?
121643.e: The WHO recommends rubbing in the product for 20 to 30 seconds until the hands are dry. In this way every part of the hands is reached.
121643.m: Hand disinfection takes about half a minute.

121644.q: How many moments for hand hygiene does the WHO describe for healthcare staff?
121644.e: The moments are: before touching a patient, before clean or aseptic procedures, after contact with body fluids, after touching a patient and after touching the patient's surroundings.
121644.m: The WHO names five moments for hand hygiene.

121645.q: What is the federal strategy for monitoring, preventing and fighting hospital infections called?
121645.e: The Federal Council adopted the NOSO strategy in 2016. It aims to reduce infections in hospitals and care homes in Switzerland.
121645.m: The NOSO strategy fights hospital infections in Switzerland.

121646.q: Why are patients in intensive care especially at risk of hospital infections?
a: They often have catheters, tubes and a weakened immune system
They always lie in single rooms
121646.e: Breathing tubes and venous catheters open direct routes into the body for germs. In addition, the defences of seriously ill people are often weakened.
121646.m: Intensive care patients have a high risk of infection.

121647.q: According to today's definition, what is sepsis?
a: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a misdirected response to an infection
Harmless reddening of the skin after an insect bite
121647.e: Since the Sepsis-3 definition of 2016, the focus is not on the infection itself but on the excessive and harmful reaction of the body. It can make organs such as the kidneys, lungs or circulation fail.
121647.m: In sepsis, the defence reaction damages the body's own organs.

121648.q: Which everyday expression is often used for sepsis?
121648.e: The term blood poisoning is widespread but inaccurate, as there is no poison in the strict sense. Lockjaw is an everyday name for tetanus.
121648.m: In everyday language, sepsis is called blood poisoning.

121649.q: Which signs during an infection can point to the start of sepsis?
121649.e: If a sick person breathes noticeably fast, seems confused or has low blood pressure, sepsis may be present. Then medical help is needed immediately.
121649.m: Fast breathing and confusion during an infection are warning signs.

121650.q: What is typical of septic shock?
a: A drop in blood pressure that needs circulation-supporting drugs despite fluids
High fever with no other symptoms
121650.e: In septic shock, the circulation is so badly disturbed that vasopressors are needed despite drips. The death rate is then especially high.
121650.m: Septic shock is the most severe form of sepsis.

121651.q: According to guidelines, within what time should antibiotics be given if septic shock is suspected?
a: Only after all lab results are in
121651.e: With every hour of delay, the risk of death rises considerably. That is why international guidelines recommend giving antibiotics within the first hour if possible.

121652.q: According to a large study in “The Lancet”, roughly how many deaths worldwide in 2017 were due to sepsis?
121652.e: The study estimated around 49 million cases of sepsis and about 11 million deaths for 2017. That was around one fifth of all deaths worldwide.
121652.m: Sepsis is one of the most common causes of death worldwide.

121653.q: Which people have an especially high risk of developing sepsis?
a: Babies, older people and people with weak immune systems
121653.e: In very young, old or immunocompromised people, the defence system is less able to contain an infection. Sepsis is therefore more common in them.
121653.m: Very young, old and immunocompromised people are especially at risk.

121654.q: Which blood value is measured in sepsis as a sign that the tissues are not getting enough oxygen?
121654.e: When cells lack oxygen, they get energy anaerobically and produce lactate. A raised lactate level shows a dangerous circulatory disorder.
121654.m: A high lactate level warns of a lack of oxygen in the tissues.

121655.q: If sepsis is suspected, what should be taken if possible before the first dose of antibiotics?
a: A saliva sample for a genetic test
121655.e: In blood cultures, the germs can be grown and tested for resistance. After antibiotics have been given, they often no longer grow, so the blood is taken beforehand.
121655.m: Blood cultures help to find the germ causing sepsis.

121656.q: In which year did the WHO declare the spread of COVID-19 a pandemic?
121656.e: On 11 March 2020, the WHO classified the worldwide spread of the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 as a pandemic. The first cases had appeared in China at the end of 2019.
121656.m: The WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic in March 2020.

121657.q: On which day did the WHO constitution come into force in 1948, a day now marked as World Health Day?
121657.e: The WHO constitution came into force on 7 April 1948. Since then, World Health Day has been held every year on this day with a focus theme.
121657.m: World Health Day is on 7 April.

121658.q: Which list has the WHO published regularly since 1977 as a guide for healthcare?
a: The Model List of Essential Medicines
The list of World Heritage Sites
The Red List of Threatened Species
The list of banned doping substances
121658.e: The model list names medicines that are important for basic healthcare in every country. It is revised about every two years.
121658.m: The WHO keeps a list of essential medicines.

121659.q: Who is Director-General of the WHO (as of 2026)?
121659.e: The Ethiopian Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has led the WHO since 2017 and was re-elected in 2022. Margaret Chan was his predecessor, and António Guterres is UN Secretary-General.
121659.m: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus leads the WHO.

121660.q: What is the highest decision-making body of the WHO, in which all member states are represented, called?
121660.e: The World Health Assembly meets every year in Geneva and sets the WHO's policy and budget. The Security Council is a body of the UN.
121660.m: The World Health Assembly is the highest body of the WHO.

121661.q: What status does the WHO have in the United Nations system?
a: It is a specialised agency of the UN
It is an authority of the European Union
121661.e: The WHO is a legally independent specialised agency of the United Nations with its own member states. It coordinates international health work.
121661.m: The WHO belongs to the UN as a specialised agency.

121662.q: Why does the WHO call for antibiotics to be used only in a targeted and sparing way?
a: So that fewer resistant bacteria develop
Because antibiotics only work in winter
Because there are hardly any antibiotics left worldwide
121662.e: Every use of antibiotics favours bacteria that are not affected by them. If resistance becomes more common, the medicines no longer work for dangerous infections.
121662.m: Using antibiotics sparingly slows down resistance.

121663.q: How does the WHO constitution define health?
a: As a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being
As simply the absence of illness
As the ability to work fully
As the result of regular visits to the doctor
121663.e: The definition in the constitution stresses that health is more than the absence of disease or infirmity. It includes mental and social well-being.
121663.m: For the WHO, health is more than the absence of illness.

121664.q: Light with a wavelength of 600 nm falls on a double slit with a slit separation of 0.3 mm. How far apart are neighbouring bright fringes on a screen 2 m away?
121664.e: For small angles, fringe spacing equals wavelength times screen distance divided by slit separation. So 600 nm · 2 m / 0.3 mm = 0.004 m = 4 mm.
121664.m: The fringe spacing grows with wavelength and screen distance.

121665.q: What path difference between the two partial waves leads to a bright fringe with a double slit?
a: An odd multiple of half the wavelength
Exactly a quarter of the wavelength
121665.e: With a path difference of k times lambda, crest meets crest and the waves reinforce each other. With an offset of half a wavelength, on the other hand, they cancel out.
121665.m: Bright fringes form when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.

121666.q: Which property of light does the fringe pattern behind a double slit prove?
121666.e: Alternating bright and dark fringes can only come from interference, the overlapping of waves. Pure particles would produce two bright stripes behind the slits.
121666.m: The interference pattern shows that light behaves like a wave.

121667.q: What do you observe if you send electrons through a double slit one at a time?
a: After many electrons, an interference pattern forms
Each electron splits into two halves
121667.e: Each electron lands at a single point, but the hits are distributed according to an interference pattern. This is a key example of wave-particle duality.
121667.m: Even single electrons show wave behaviour.

121668.q: What happens to the interference pattern if you measure which slit each particle goes through?
a: The pattern becomes twice as bright
121668.e: As soon as there is which-way information, the two possibilities can no longer interfere. What remains is a distribution like that of classical particles.
121668.m: Measuring the path destroys the interference.

121669.q: How does the spacing of the bright fringes change if you double the slit separation and change nothing else?
121669.e: The fringe spacing is inversely proportional to the slit separation. So double the slit separation gives half the fringe spacing.
121669.m: A greater slit separation gives narrower fringes.

121670.q: Which light produces the most widely spaced fringes with the same double slit?
121670.e: Red light has the longest wavelength of the colours listed. Since the fringe spacing is proportional to the wavelength, its fringes are furthest apart.
121670.m: Long-wavelength light gives wider interference fringes.

121671.q: Behind a double slit with a slit separation of 0.2 mm, the bright fringes on a screen 1 m away are 3 mm apart. What is the wavelength of the light?
121671.e: Wavelength equals fringe spacing times slit separation divided by screen distance. So 3 mm · 0.2 mm / 1 m = 0.0000006 m = 600 nm.
121671.m: The double slit can be used to measure the wavelength of light.

121672.q: When did Thomas Young present his interference experiments with light?
a: At the beginning of the 19th century
In the middle of the 17th century
At the end of the 18th century
At the beginning of the 20th century
121672.e: Young published his work on interference in London between 1801 and 1803. It was among the most important evidence for the wave nature of light.
121672.m: Thomas Young showed the interference of light around 1801.

121673.q: Whose particle theory of light did Thomas Young call into question with his experiments?
121673.e: Newton’s corpuscular theory described light as a stream of tiny particles and was the dominant view at the time. Huygens, on the other hand, had already put forward a wave theory, which Young supported.
121673.m: Young strengthened the wave theory against Newton’s particle picture.

121674.q: Thomas Young made important contributions to deciphering which script?
121674.e: Young studied the Rosetta Stone and recognised that certain hieroglyphs stand for sounds. The full decipherment was achieved by Jean-François Champollion in 1822.
121674.m: Thomas Young also worked on hieroglyphs.

121675.q: Which material property is called “Young’s modulus” in English after Thomas Young?
121675.e: The modulus of elasticity tells you how much a material deforms under tension or compression. A high value means a stiff material such as steel.
121675.m: In English, the modulus of elasticity bears Young’s name.

121676.q: Which theory of colour vision goes back to Thomas Young and Hermann von Helmholtz?
121676.e: According to the Young-Helmholtz theory, the eye has three kinds of colour receptors for red, green and blue. All colours come from their different levels of stimulation.
121676.m: The eye sees colours with three types of receptor.

121677.q: What profession did Thomas Young have alongside his research?
121677.e: Young studied medicine, including in Göttingen, and worked as a doctor in London. His knowledge of the eye fed into his research on optics.
121677.m: Thomas Young was a doctor by profession.

121678.q: Which part of Britain was Thomas Young from?
121678.e: Thomas Young was born in 1773 in Milverton in the English county of Somerset. He died in London in 1829.

121679.q: Which experiment did Thomas Young use to show the wave nature of light?
121679.e: Light behind two narrow slits forms bright and dark fringes. This interference pattern can only be explained by waves.
121679.m: The double slit shows that light interferes.

121680.q: Which equation describes the position of the maxima for an optical grating with grating spacing g?
121680.e: A maximum forms when the path difference between neighbouring slits, g · sin α, is a whole number of wavelengths. k is the order of the maximum.
121680.m: For a grating, g times sin alpha equals k times lambda.

121681.q: Which of these gratings deflects light of the same wavelength most strongly in the first order?
a: A grating with 1200 lines per mm
A grating with 600 lines per mm
A grating with 300 lines per mm
A grating with 100 lines per mm
121681.e: More lines per millimetre mean a smaller grating spacing. According to sin α = λ / g, the angle then becomes larger.
121681.m: The more lines per millimetre, the stronger the diffraction.

121682.q: A grating has a spacing of 2 µm. Up to which order at most can maxima be observed for light of 600 nm?
121682.e: Since sin α is at most 1, k is at most g / λ = 2 µm / 600 nm, about 3.3. So the highest whole order is 3.
121682.m: The sine limits the number of grating orders.

121683.q: Why are the maxima of a grating much sharper than with a double slit?
a: Because very many slits interfere at the same time
Because the grating focuses light like a lens
Because the grating only lets one colour through
121683.e: With many slits, the waves cancel out almost completely even at small deviations from the angle of the maximum. What remains are narrow, bright lines.

121684.q: An optical grating has 500 lines per millimetre. What is its grating spacing?
121684.e: The grating spacing is the distance between neighbouring lines: 1 mm / 500 = 0.002 mm. That is 2 µm.
121684.m: The grating spacing is the reciprocal of the number of lines per length.

121685.q: What colour is the zero-order maximum when white light falls on a grating?
121685.e: In the zero order, the path difference is zero for all wavelengths. All the colours overlap there again to give white light.
121685.m: The central maximum of a grating stays white.

121686.q: Why does the underside of a CD shimmer in rainbow colours?
a: The closely spaced data tracks act as a reflection grating
The plastic layer acts as a prism
The light is converted by fluorescence
121686.e: The tracks of a CD are about 1.6 µm apart. The reflected light interferes as at a grating and is fanned out by wavelength.
121686.m: A CD acts like an optical grating.

121687.q: How can you better separate two very similar wavelengths with an optical grating?
a: By placing the screen closer to the grating
121687.e: The resolving power of a grating is the product of the order and the number of lines illuminated. The more lines take part, the sharper the lines become.
121687.m: More lines and a higher order separate wavelengths better.

121688.q: A 633 nm laser produces the first-order maximum at 30 degrees with a grating. What is the grating spacing?
121688.e: From g · sin α = λ, g = 633 nm / sin 30° = 633 nm / 0.5. That gives 1266 nm, about 1.27 µm.
121688.m: The grating spacing can be calculated from the diffraction angle.

121689.q: What does an optical spectrometer measure?
a: The intensity of light depending on wavelength
The speed of light in a vacuum
The temperature of a light source directly
121689.e: A spectrometer splits light by wavelength and measures how much light arrives at each wavelength. This gives a spectrum.
121689.m: A spectrometer splits light into its wavelengths.

121690.q: Why can a prism split light into colours?
a: The refractive index of the glass depends on the wavelength
The prism acts as a double slit
The light is diffracted at the tip
121690.e: This dependence is called dispersion. In normal glass, short-wavelength light is refracted more strongly than long-wavelength light.
121690.m: Dispersion splits light in a prism.

121691.q: Why is a spectrometer illuminated with a lamp with known lines, such as a mercury vapour lamp?
a: To remove dust from the grating
121691.e: The lines of the lamp lie at precisely known wavelengths. By matching them to the measured positions on the detector, you can assign a wavelength to every position.
121691.m: Spectrometers are calibrated with known spectral lines.

121692.q: Which component at the entrance of a spectrometer only lets in a narrow beam of light?
121692.e: The narrow entrance slit is imaged in the spectrometer. The narrower it is, the sharper the spectral lines, but the less light gets in.
121692.m: The entrance slit helps determine how sharp the lines are.

121693.q: Which detector records the whole spectrum at once in modern compact spectrometers?
a: A CCD or CMOS line sensor
121693.e: The line sensor consists of many light-sensitive pixels side by side. Each pixel measures a small range of wavelengths.
121693.m: Modern spectrometers measure with line sensors.

121694.q: Which method did the Geneva astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz use in 1995 to find the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star?
121694.e: With a high-precision spectrograph, they measured how the lines of the star 51 Pegasi shift periodically. From this they concluded that a planet was orbiting it, and they received the Nobel Prize in 2019.
121694.m: Spectrometers can find exoplanets through the wobbling of their stars.

121695.q: What is a spectrometer’s ability to show two close wavelengths separately called?
121695.e: A high spectral resolution makes it possible to separate closely spaced lines such as the sodium double line. It depends on the grating, slit and detector.
121695.m: Spectral resolution shows how finely a spectrometer separates.

121696.q: Why do spectrometers for ultraviolet often use optics made of quartz glass instead of ordinary glass?
a: Ordinary glass absorbs much of the UV light
Ordinary glass does not refract light
121696.e: Normal optical glass becomes opaque in short-wavelength ultraviolet. Quartz glass lets UV light through down to much shorter wavelengths.

121697.q: What kind of waves can be polarised?
121697.e: Polarisation describes the direction of oscillation across the direction of travel. In longitudinal waves, such as sound in air, everything oscillates in the direction of travel, so there is no polarisation.
121697.m: Only transverse waves can be polarised.

121698.q: For Brewster’s angle, tan α = n. At what angle of incidence is light reflected from glass with a refractive index of 1.5 completely polarised?
121698.e: With tan α = 1.5, α equals arctan 1.5, about 56.3 degrees.
121698.m: At Brewster’s angle, reflected light is completely polarised.

121699.q: What angle do the reflected and refracted rays form when light comes in at Brewster’s angle?
121699.e: At Brewster’s angle, the reflected and refracted rays are at right angles to each other. The dipoles in the glass then cannot radiate in the direction of the reflected ray.
121699.m: At Brewster’s angle, the rays are at right angles to each other.

121700.q: Which mineral shows such strong double refraction that you see writing double through a crystal?
121700.e: Calcite splits light into two rays polarised at right angles to each other. Especially clear pieces are called Iceland spar.

121701.q: Which animals use the polarised light of the sky to find their way?
121701.e: Bees use special visual cells to detect the polarisation pattern of the sky. This lets them find the direction of the Sun even when the sky is partly cloudy.

121702.q: Which screen technology is based on polarised light?
121702.e: In an LCD, liquid crystals rotate the direction of polarisation of the light depending on the voltage applied. Two polarising layers turn this into bright and dark pixels.
121702.m: LCD screens control light through its polarisation.

121703.q: How do many 3D cinema glasses separate the images for the left and right eye?
121703.e: The two images are projected with different polarisations. Each lens of the glasses only lets the matching image through.
121703.m: 3D glasses in the cinema use polarisation.

121704.q: How can unpolarised light be polarised without a filter?
a: By reflection from glass or water
By focusing it with a magnifying glass
121704.e: In 1808 Étienne-Louis Malus discovered that light reflected from glass or water is partly polarised. Scattering in the air also polarises skylight.
121704.m: Reflection from glass or water polarises light.

121705.e: The atoms of the Sun radiate independently of each other in all directions of oscillation. So its direct light is unpolarised; only scattering and reflection partly polarise it.

121706.q: Linearly polarised light hits a polarising filter whose transmission direction is turned by 60 degrees. What share of the intensity gets through?
121706.e: According to Malus’s law, I = I0 · cos² α. With cos 60° = 0.5, you get 0.5² = 0.25, so 25 per cent.
121706.m: Malus’s law describes how a polarising filter weakens light.

121707.q: What does a simple polarising film do to unpolarised light?
a: It only lets light of one direction of oscillation through
It only lets infrared light through
121707.e: The film contains long, aligned molecules. They absorb light oscillating parallel to them and let the perpendicular direction through. About half the light is lost this way.
121707.m: A polarising filter only lets one direction of oscillation through.

121708.q: How much light passes through two ideal polarising filters whose transmission directions are crossed at 90 degrees?
121708.e: After the first filter, the light only oscillates in one direction. The second filter only lets through exactly the perpendicular direction; cos² 90° is zero.
121708.m: Crossed polarising filters block the light.

121709.q: Unpolarised light passes through three ideal polarising filters with directions of 0, 45 and 90 degrees. What share arrives at the end?
121709.e: The first filter lets half through, and each of the next two lets through cos² 45° = 0.5. In total 0.5 · 0.5 · 0.5 = 0.125.
121709.m: A filter in the middle can make crossed polarising filters let light through again.

121710.q: What do photographers often use a polarising filter for?
a: To reduce reflections on water or glass
121710.e: Reflected light from non-metallic surfaces is partly polarised and can therefore be filtered out. The blue sky also often looks deeper.

121711.q: Why do polarising sunglasses mainly let vertically oscillating light through?
a: Because glare from horizontal surfaces is mostly horizontally polarised
Because the eye cannot see horizontal light
Because vertical light contains less UV
121711.e: Light reflected from roads, water or snow mainly oscillates parallel to the surface. The glasses block this direction and so reduce glare.
121711.m: Polarising sunglasses reduce glare from reflections.

121712.q: For which type of camera did the company Polaroid, which grew out of the invention of cheap polarising film, become famous?
121712.e: At the end of the 1920s, Edwin Land developed a cheap polarising film and founded the company Polaroid. Later it became famous mainly for instant cameras, whose photos came straight out of the camera.
121712.m: The instant camera came from the polarising filter company Polaroid.

121713.q: In photoelasticity, what do you make visible by placing a transparent plastic part between crossed polarising filters?
121713.e: Under stress, plastic becomes doubly refracting and rotates the polarisation differently depending on the wavelength. Coloured patterns appear that reveal stress peaks.
121713.m: Polarising filters make stresses in plastic visible in colour.

121714.q: Why do soap bubbles shimmer in bright colours?
a: Light reflected from the front and back of the film interferes
The air in the bubble glows
The bubble refracts light like a prism
121714.e: Depending on the thickness of the soap film, certain wavelengths are reinforced and others cancel out. Because the thickness varies, changing colours appear.
121714.m: Soap bubbles shimmer because of interference.

121715.q: What happens to a light wave that is reflected at an optically denser medium?
a: It undergoes a phase jump of half a wavelength
121715.e: On reflection at a denser medium, the oscillation reverses, which corresponds to a path difference of λ/2. At a less dense medium there is no such jump.
121715.m: Reflection at a denser medium shifts the phase by half a wave.

121716.q: What is the minimum thickness of an anti-reflective coating with a refractive index of 1.38 for light of 550 nm?
121716.e: The coating should be a quarter of the wavelength in the material thick: 550 nm / (4 · 1.38) gives about 99.6 nm. The two reflected waves are then half a wavelength apart and cancel out.
121716.m: Anti-reflective coatings are a quarter of a wavelength thick.

121717.q: Why does a soap film look black at the top just before it bursts?
a: It is much thinner than the wavelength, and the reflected waves cancel out
The soap burns at that spot
The light is completely absorbed there
121717.e: When the thickness almost disappears, only the phase jump of half a wavelength at the front surface remains. Both reflections are in antiphase, and no colour is reflected.
121717.m: Very thin soap films look black.

121718.q: What is the ring pattern called that forms when a slightly curved lens lies on a flat glass plate?
121718.e: Between the lens and the plate there is a wedge of air whose thickness increases outwards. At certain thicknesses the light is reinforced or cancelled, which gives concentric rings.
121718.m: Newton’s rings form in a thin air gap.

121719.q: A soap film with a refractive index of 1.33 is 100 nm thick. Which wavelength is reinforced most in reflection when light falls on it at right angles?
121719.e: Because of the phase jump at the front surface, reinforcement requires 2 · n · d = (m + 1/2) · λ. With m = 0, λ = 2 · 1.33 · 100 nm / 0.5 = 532 nm.
121719.m: The film thickness determines the colour of thin films.

121720.q: Where does the shimmering blue of the wings of some morpho butterflies come from?
a: From interference at fine layered structures in the scales
From blue pigment in the scales
121720.e: The wing scales contain tiny layered structures spaced at distances similar to light wavelengths. Blue light is reflected more strongly there by interference; this is called structural colour.
121720.m: Morpho butterflies shine because of structural colours.

121721.q: Why does a thin film of oil on a wet road shimmer in colours?
a: Light interferes at the top and bottom of the oil film
The asphalt glows through the oil
121721.e: The oil film is only a few hundred nanometres thick, and its thickness varies. At each spot, a different wavelength is reflected more strongly.
121721.m: Oil films shimmer because of thin-film interference.

121722.q: How does the strength of Rayleigh scattering depend on the wavelength λ?
a: It does not depend on λ
121722.e: The intensity of scattering by very small particles grows with the fourth power of the frequency. So short-wavelength light is scattered much more strongly.
121722.m: Rayleigh scattering strongly favours short-wavelength light.

121723.q: By what factor is light of 400 nm scattered more strongly by air molecules than light of 700 nm?
121723.e: The ratio is (700 / 400) to the power of 4. That gives 1.75⁴, about 9.4.
121723.m: Violet light is scattered almost ten times more strongly than red.

121725.q: Why does the Sun look reddish at sunset?
a: The light travels a long way through the air, and blue is scattered out
The Sun cools down in the evening
The Earth reflects red light back
The eye becomes more sensitive to red in the evening
121725.e: When the Sun is low, the light’s path through the atmosphere is much longer. Along the way, almost all the blue part is scattered sideways, leaving yellow, orange and red.
121725.m: The red evening sky occurs because blue is lost along the way.

121726.q: Why are clouds and fog white and not blue like the sky?
a: Their droplets scatter all colours roughly equally
Their droplets absorb blue light completely
Water droplets glow white by themselves
Clouds reflect the snow on the ground
121726.e: Water droplets are much larger than air molecules. Such large particles scatter light almost independently of wavelength, and all the colours together make white.
121726.m: Large droplets scatter all colours equally, so clouds are white.

121727.q: For the discovery of which element did Lord Rayleigh receive the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1904?
121727.e: Rayleigh found that nitrogen obtained from air was slightly heavier than nitrogen made chemically. Together with William Ramsay, this led him to discover the noble gas argon in 1894.
121727.m: Lord Rayleigh was a co-discoverer of argon.

121728.q: At what angle to the Sun is scattered skylight most strongly polarised?
121728.e: Scattering by molecules produces the strongest polarisation at a scattering angle of 90 degrees. With a polarising filter, the sky gets noticeably darker there.
121728.m: At right angles to the Sun, skylight is strongly polarised.

121729.q: Why do we see the sky as blue and not violet, even though violet is scattered even more strongly?
a: Sunlight contains less violet and the eye is not very sensitive to it
Violet light is swallowed by clouds
Violet light does not reach the Earth at all
Violet light is only scattered at night
121729.e: The solar spectrum is weaker in the violet, and some of it is absorbed high in the atmosphere. In addition, our cone cells respond only weakly to violet.
121729.m: The solar spectrum and the eye make the sky blue instead of violet.

121730.q: What is the frequency of green light with a wavelength of 500 nm?
121730.e: f = c / λ = 3 · 10⁸ m/s / (5 · 10⁻⁷ m). That gives 6 · 10¹⁴ Hz.
121730.m: Visible light oscillates hundreds of trillions of times a second.

121731.q: What is the range of electromagnetic waves with frequencies from about 300 MHz to 300 GHz called?
121731.e: Microwaves have wavelengths of about 1 mm to 1 m. They are used for radar, mobile phones, Wi-Fi and microwave ovens.
121731.m: Microwaves lie between radio waves and infrared.

121732.q: What is the wavelength of an FM radio station at 100 MHz?
121732.m: FM radio waves are a few metres long.

121733.q: A microwave oven works at 2.45 GHz. Roughly what is the wavelength?
121733.e: λ = c / f = 300,000,000 m/s / 2,450,000,000 Hz gives about 0.122 m. That is about 12 cm.
121733.m: Household microwaves are about 12 centimetres long.

121734.q: Roughly what energy does a photon with a wavelength of 500 nm have?
121734.e: E = h · c / λ. With h · c about 1240 eV · nm, E = 1240 / 500 eV, about 2.5 eV.
121734.m: Photons of visible light carry a few electronvolts.

121735.q: Roughly what energy does an X-ray photon with a wavelength of 0.1 nm have?
121735.e: With E = h · c / λ and h · c about 1240 eV · nm, E = 1240 / 0.1 eV = 12,400 eV. That is about 12 keV.
121735.m: A short wavelength means high photon energy.

121736.q: Who first demonstrated electromagnetic waves in an experiment in the 1880s?
121736.e: Hertz produced waves with a spark transmitter and detected them with a receiving ring. The unit of frequency is named after him.
121736.m: Heinrich Hertz proved electromagnetic waves experimentally.

121737.q: Which radiation does a thermal imaging camera make visible?
121737.e: Bodies at room temperature radiate mainly in the infrared at about 10 µm. The camera turns this radiation into a visible false-colour image.
121737.m: Thermal imaging cameras see infrared radiation.

121738.q: From which part of the spectrum can radiation ionise atoms?
121738.e: To ionise, a photon usually needs a few electronvolts to over 10 eV. Short-wavelength UV, X-rays and gamma rays reach this energy.
121738.m: Ionising radiation begins in the short-wavelength ultraviolet.

121739.q: What kind of spectrum does a glowing gas of low density give off?
121739.e: The atoms of a thin gas only radiate at certain wavelengths that match their energy levels. Glowing solids, on the other hand, give a continuous spectrum.

121740.q: How does an emission line form in an atom?
a: An electron moves to a lower energy level and gives off a photon
A proton leaves the atomic nucleus
The atom splits into two atoms
An electron takes up a photon
121740.e: The photon energy matches exactly the difference between the two energy levels. Because these levels are fixed for each element, sharp lines form.
121740.m: Emission lines form when an electron jumps down.

121741.q: Which element gives fireworks a strong red colour?
121741.e: Strontium compounds mainly give off red light when heated. Copper colours blue to green, barium green and sodium yellow.

121742.q: Roughly what is the wavelength of the light when the hydrogen electron moves from n = 4 to n = 2?
121742.e: According to the Balmer formula, 1/λ = R · (1/4 − 1/16), with R equal to 1.097 · 10⁷ per metre. From this, λ is about 486 nm, a blue-green line.
121742.m: In the visible range, hydrogen gives off the Balmer lines.

121743.q: In which part of the spectrum is the Lyman series of hydrogen?
121743.e: The Lyman series comes from transitions to the ground level n = 1. These jumps carry a lot of energy, so the lines are in the ultraviolet.
121743.m: The Lyman series lies in the ultraviolet.

121744.q: What did Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff make possible with the spectral analysis they developed?
a: Identifying elements by their spectral lines
Measuring the temperature of the Earth
121744.e: Every element gives off a typical line spectrum when heated, like a fingerprint. Bunsen and Kirchhoff even discovered new elements this way, such as caesium and rubidium.
121744.m: Spectral lines are an element’s fingerprint.

121745.q: Which element was first discovered in the spectrum of the Sun in 1868, before it was found on Earth?
121745.e: During a solar eclipse, an unknown yellow line was noticed in the spectrum of the solar prominences. The element was named after the Greek word helios for Sun.
121745.m: Helium was first discovered on the Sun.

121746.q: Why does a tube filled with neon glow red-orange?
a: The strongest emission lines of neon are in the red range
The glass of the tube is coloured red
The current only flows when the colour is red
121746.e: In the tube, electric current excites the neon atoms. When they fall back, they give off their typical line spectrum, which is dominated by red lines.
121746.m: Every gas glows in its own colours.

121747.q: How does an absorption spectrum form?
a: Light with a continuous spectrum passes through a cooler gas
A hot gas glows against a dark background
Light is reflected by a mirror
121747.e: The atoms of the gas take up exactly those photons whose energy matches the differences between their levels. These wavelengths are then missing from the spectrum as dark lines.
121747.m: An absorption spectrum shows dark lines in a rainbow.

121748.q: What does Kirchhoff's law of radiation say about the spectral lines of a gas?
a: A gas absorbs the same wavelengths that it also emits
A gas emits only wavelengths that it does not absorb
A gas absorbs all wavelengths equally strongly
121748.e: The absorption and emission lines of an element lie in the same places. This is why dark lines let you work out what a gas is made of.
121748.m: A gas swallows exactly the colours that it can give off itself.

121749.q: Which parts of the light does chlorophyll absorb particularly strongly?
121749.e: Chlorophyll has absorption peaks in the blue and red ranges. Green light is hardly absorbed and is reflected, which is why leaves look green.
121749.m: Leaves are green because chlorophyll hardly absorbs green.

121750.q: A sample has an absorbance of 2. What fraction of the light is let through?
121750.e: Absorbance is the negative base-10 logarithm of the transmittance. With an absorbance of 2 the transmittance is 10 to the power of -2, so 1 per cent.
121750.m: Each unit of absorbance weakens the light by a factor of ten.

121751.q: According to the Beer-Lambert law, how does the absorbance of a coloured solution change if you double its concentration?
121751.e: Absorbance is proportional to concentration and to path length. Twice as many dissolved particles absorb correspondingly more light.
121751.m: The Beer-Lambert law is used to determine concentrations.

121752.q: In which part of the spectrum do carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb strongly, leading to the greenhouse effect?
121752.e: The Earth's surface gives off heat as infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb some of it and radiate part of it back to Earth.

121753.q: Which gas in the stratosphere absorbs a large part of the Sun's UV radiation?
121753.e: Ozone molecules absorb especially the dangerous UV-B and UV-C radiation. In this way the ozone layer protects living things on Earth.
121753.m: The ozone layer filters out UV radiation.

121754.q: Why does a pane of glass with red dye look red in white light?
a: It absorbs the other colours and mainly lets red through
It turns all colours into red
121754.e: Colour filters work by absorption. Whatever part of the white light is not absorbed reaches the eye and determines the colour.
121754.m: Colour filters only let their own colour through.

121755.q: Which optician described more than 500 dark lines in the solar spectrum in 1814?
121755.e: Joseph von Fraunhofer studied sunlight with prisms and telescopes he built himself. He labelled the most important lines with letters from A to K.
121755.m: Fraunhofer mapped the dark lines in the solar spectrum.

121756.q: What do you call a spectrum that consists of a coloured band with dark lines, like the solar spectrum?
121756.e: The dark lines appear because gases filter certain wavelengths out of the light. An emission spectrum, by contrast, shows bright lines on a dark background.
121756.m: Dark lines in a coloured band form an absorption spectrum.

a: Absorption in the outer gas layers of the Sun
Dust between the Sun and the Earth
121757.e: The continuous light from deeper layers passes through cooler gases in the Sun's atmosphere. Their atoms absorb certain wavelengths.
121757.m: Fraunhofer lines reveal what the Sun is made of.

121758.q: Which element causes the Fraunhofer double line D at about 589 nm?
121758.e: The two D lines lie at about 589.0 and 589.6 nm. The same lines glow yellow in sodium vapour lamps.
121758.m: The D lines come from sodium.

121759.q: Which element was first discovered in 1868 through a line in the solar spectrum, before it was found on Earth?
121759.e: During a solar eclipse, astronomers observed a yellow line that did not match any known element. The new element was named after the Greek word for sun, helios.
121759.m: Helium was first discovered on the Sun.

121760.q: Which two scientists showed around 1859 that every chemical element has its own spectral lines?
121760.e: Kirchhoff and Bunsen studied flames containing different substances and so founded spectral analysis. This made it possible to match the Fraunhofer lines to particular elements in the Sun.
121760.m: Kirchhoff and Bunsen founded spectral analysis.

121761.q: Why are the dark Fraunhofer lines exactly where the same gases show bright lines when hot?
a: Atoms absorb exactly the wavelengths that they also emit
The Earth casts a shadow there
Bright light is turned into heat in the Sun
121761.e: Each atom can only take up or give off certain portions of energy. That is why the absorption and emission lines of an element match.
121761.m: Atoms swallow the same colours that they also give off.

121762.q: What follows if the absorption lines in the spectrum of a distant galaxy are shifted towards the red?
a: The galaxy is moving away from us
The galaxy is coming towards us
The galaxy is colder than the Sun
121762.e: Redshift shows that the galaxy is moving away. Edwin Hubble found that more distant galaxies are more strongly redshifted, a sign that the universe is expanding.
121762.m: Redshifted lines show a galaxy moving away.

121763.q: Besides the prism, which optical device was Fraunhofer one of the first to make, so that he could split light even more precisely?
121763.e: A diffraction grating consists of a great many fine, parallel lines. With it, Fraunhofer was able to measure the wavelengths of the dark lines for the first time.
121763.m: A diffraction grating lets you measure wavelengths precisely.

121764.q: What does limnology deal with as a science?
a: Inland waters such as lakes and rivers
121764.e: Limnology is the science of inland waters. It studies lakes, ponds, rivers and streams as ecosystems.

121765.q: What do you study when you assess the health of a lake?
a: Oxygen, nutrients and living things in the water
Only the colour of the sand on the shore
Only the air temperature above the lake
121765.e: Experts measure things such as oxygen, phosphorus and visibility depth and record algae, small animals and fish. Only together do these give a picture of the state of the lake.
121765.m: A lake is assessed on the basis of its chemistry and its living things.

121766.q: To which lake did François-Alphonse Forel devote his three-volume main work?
121766.e: His work “Le Léman” describes Lake Geneva in terms of physics, chemistry and biology. It is regarded as the first comprehensive monograph on a lake.
121766.m: Forel’s main work is called “Le Léman”.

121767.q: What is a standing wave called in which the whole surface of a lake swings back and forth?
121767.e: In a seiche, the water of a lake sloshes back and forth as in a bathtub. Forel was one of the first to study this phenomenon closely.
121767.m: A seiche is a rocking wave of a whole lake.

121768.q: What is the habitat of the open water of a lake, away from the shore and the bottom, called?
121768.e: The pelagic zone is the open-water zone. Plankton and free-swimming fish such as whitefish live there.
121768.m: The pelagic zone is the open-water zone of a lake.

121769.q: What is the dark deep zone of the lake bed below the littoral zone called?
121769.e: The profundal zone is the deep lake bed that no longer receives enough light for plants. There, mainly bacteria and bottom-dwelling animals break down material that has sunk down.
121769.m: The profundal zone is the dark lake bed in the depths.

121770.q: Which device is used to measure the visibility depth of a lake?
121770.e: A white or black-and-white disc is lowered on a line. The depth at which it just disappears is the visibility depth.
121770.m: Visibility depth is measured with a Secchi disc.

121771.q: What is the depth called at which the photosynthesis of algae just balances their own respiration?
121771.e: Above the compensation depth, algae produce more oxygen than they use. Below it, consumption outweighs production.
121771.m: At the compensation depth, photosynthesis and respiration balance each other.

121772.q: Why does a fast-flowing mountain stream usually contain more oxygen than a warm pond?
a: Cold, moving water takes up more oxygen
More trees grow in the stream
121772.e: Cold water can dissolve more gas than warm water. Eddies and waves also keep bringing air into the water.
121772.m: Cold, moving water is rich in oxygen.

121773.q: What is the phase called in which a lake is stably layered in summer and does not mix?
121773.e: During summer stagnation, warm water lies stably on top of cold water. This phase only ends in autumn when the water cools.
121773.m: In summer, a layered lake stagnates.

121774.q: What is the cold, dense deep layer of a lake that is layered in summer called?
121774.e: The hypolimnion lies below the thermocline and stays cold all summer. It is cut off from exchange with the air.
121774.m: The hypolimnion is the cold deep layer.

121775.q: Roughly what temperature is the water at the bottom of a frozen, deep lake in winter?
121775.e: Water is densest at around 4 °C and therefore sinks to the bottom. The colder water near 0 °C stays just below the ice.
121775.m: Under the ice, the deep water is about 4 °C.

121776.q: What is the layering under a covering of ice called, in which the colder water is on top?
121776.e: In winter, water near 0 °C lies above the denser water at 4 °C. This reversed order is called inverse stratification.
121776.m: In winter under ice, the stratification is inverse.

121777.q: Why is summer stratification in a lake very stable, even though the temperature difference is only a few degrees?
a: At higher temperatures, density changes more per degree
The sun pushes the warm water down
The ice holds the layers in place
121777.e: The warmer the water, the bigger the difference in density per degree. That is why the wind needs a great deal of energy in summer to mix the layers.
121777.m: In summer, warm water lies very stably on top of cold water.

121778.q: How does global warming affect the summer stratification of many Swiss lakes?
a: It starts earlier and lasts longer
It only occurs in winter now
121778.e: Warmer surfaces lead to earlier and more stable stratification. This makes mixing, and therefore the supply of oxygen to the depths, more difficult.
121778.m: Global warming lengthens the stratification of lakes.

121779.q: Which process mainly mixes the epilimnion of a lake?
121779.e: Wind creates waves and currents that mix the upper layer. That is why the epilimnion usually has an almost uniform temperature.
121779.m: The wind mixes the upper layer of water.

121780.q: What is the state called in which a lake has the same temperature from top to bottom?
121780.e: With homothermy, there is no longer any difference in density between the layers. Then the wind can turn over the whole lake.
121780.m: When the temperature is the same everywhere, it is called homothermy.

121781.q: What is the technical name for the layer of a lake that lies between the warm surface layer and the cold deep water?
121781.e: The metalimnion lies between the warm surface layer and the cold deep water. In it, the temperature drops sharply with depth.
121781.m: The middle layer with the temperature drop is called the metalimnion.

121782.q: What is the zone of steepest temperature drop called, a term used for lakes as well as oceans?
121782.e: The thermocline is the zone with the steepest temperature gradient. The term is used for lakes and oceans.
121782.m: The thermocline is the zone of steepest temperature drop.

121783.q: Which temperature gradient is often used as a criterion for the thermocline?
121783.e: A common definition requires a temperature drop of at least one degree per metre of depth. In deep lakes, this zone is often only a few metres thick.
121783.m: In the thermocline, the temperature falls by at least one degree per metre.

121784.q: Why does hardly any oxygen from the air reach the deep water of a stratified lake in summer?
a: The deep water is too salty
The algae lock up all the oxygen
121784.e: The thermocline acts like a barrier, because water of different densities hardly mixes. That is why the oxygen in the deep water can only decrease during the summer.
121784.m: The thermocline separates the deep water from the air.

121785.q: What is a layer of sudden change called that is caused by a change in salt content?
121785.e: In a halocline, the salt content changes abruptly with depth. It is found, for example, in the sea or in fjords.
121785.m: A halocline is a layer where the salt content changes sharply.

121786.q: Which property of water changes sharply at every such layer, whether it is caused by temperature or salt content?
121786.e: Colder and saltier water is denser. So every temperature or salt layer is also a density layer, which experts call a pycnocline. It slows down mixing.
121786.m: Every thermocline or halocline is also a density layer.

121787.q: What happens to the thermocline of a lake when the surface cools in autumn?
a: It rises to the surface and freezes
It becomes thicker and more stable
121787.e: Cooling and autumn storms deepen the mixed layer. In the end the thermocline disappears and the lake can circulate.

121788.q: What effect does a thermocline in the sea have for submerged submarines?
a: It deflects sound waves and makes detection harder
It supplies oxygen for the crew
121788.e: Sound waves are refracted at the thermocline. A submarine below this layer is therefore harder to find with sonar.
121788.m: A thermocline can deflect sonar signals.

121789.q: What is a lake called that mixes completely twice a year?
121789.e: Dimictic lakes circulate in spring and in autumn. In between they are stratified, in summer and under the winter ice.
121789.m: A dimictic lake mixes twice a year.

121790.q: What is a lake called whose deep water permanently does not mix with the rest of the water?
121790.e: In meromictic lakes, a deep layer is permanently excluded from exchange. It is often without oxygen.
121790.m: A meromictic lake never mixes completely.

121791.q: Why is the deep water of a lake that never mixes completely often without oxygen?
a: It gets no oxygen from the surface, but decomposition uses it up
It is too warm for oxygen
Fish breathe away all the oxygen
121791.e: Oxygen reaches the depths from the surface when the lake mixes. Without mixing, bacteria use up what is left as they break down dead material.
121791.m: Without mixing, the deep water becomes low in oxygen.

121792.q: What is a lake called that mixes completely very often, for example in every storm, because it is shallow?
121792.e: Shallow lakes cannot build up stable stratification. They are often turned over by the wind right down to the bottom and are called polymictic.

121793.q: Why do deep lakes such as Lake Geneva not mix right down to the bottom every winter?
a: In mild winters the water does not cool enough
The ice cover blocks all wind
The rivers flowing in are too warm in winter
121793.e: For complete mixing, the surface must become almost as cold as the deep water. In mild winters, the cooling is not enough for this in deep Lake Geneva.
121793.m: Deep lakes only mix completely in cold winters.

121794.q: What mainly reaches the depths of a lake during complete turnover?
121794.e: During turnover, water enriched with oxygen from the air sinks down. At the same time, nutrients rise from the depths.
121794.m: Turnover brings oxygen into the depths.

121795.q: In which direction do dissolved nutrients such as phosphate mainly move during lake turnover?
a: From the shore into the groundwater
From the air into the lake
From the top into the sediment
121795.e: Nutrients build up in the deep water through decomposition. During turnover, they reach the sunlit zone and boost algal growth in spring.
121795.m: Turnover brings nutrients up from the depths.

121796.q: What is a lake called that never mixes at all, for example because it is permanently frozen?
121796.e: Amictic lakes are permanently covered with ice, for example in Antarctica. The wind cannot turn their water over.

121797.q: What does the trophic state of a lake describe?
a: Its supply of nutrients and its productivity
121797.e: The trophic state shows how many nutrients a body of water contains and how much biomass it produces. It ranges from oligotrophic to hypertrophic.
121797.m: The trophic state measures the nutrient supply of a body of water.

121798.q: Which order of trophic levels from nutrient-poor to nutrient-rich is correct?
121798.e: “Oligo” means little, “meso” middle, “eu” good and “hyper” excessive. So the nutrient supply rises in this order.
121798.m: The trophic levels rise from oligotrophic to hypertrophic.

121799.q: What is a nutrient-poor bog lake coloured brown by humic substances called?
121799.e: Dystrophic waters contain many humic substances from bogs. The water is brownish and acidic, and production is low.
121799.m: Brown bog waters are called dystrophic.

121800.q: Which measurement is often used as a measure of the amount of algae when determining the trophic state?
121800.e: Chlorophyll a is found in all algae. Its concentration in the water therefore shows how much phytoplankton is present.
121800.m: Chlorophyll a indicates the amount of algae.

121801.q: Which nutrient was the main reason for the over-fertilisation of many Swiss lakes in the 1960s and 1970s?
121801.e: Phosphate from waste water and detergents made algae grow massively. The Swiss researcher Richard Vollenweider showed how the phosphorus input determines a lake’s trophic state. Phosphates in detergents were banned in 1986.
121801.m: Phosphorus was the main reason for over-fertilised lakes.

121802.q: Which cyanobacterium sometimes turns some Swiss lakes, such as Lake Murten, reddish?
121802.e: The burgundy blood alga (Planktothrix rubescens) forms red blooms in nutrient-rich lakes. Its German name recalls the legend of the blood of the Burgundians after the Battle of Murten.
121802.m: The burgundy blood alga can turn lakes red.

121803.q: How does the oxygen concentration in the hypolimnion of a eutrophic lake change over the summer?
a: It fluctuates in a daily rhythm
121803.e: Algae that sink down are broken down in the deep water, using up oxygen. During summer stratification, hardly any new oxygen comes from above.
121803.m: In eutrophic lakes, oxygen disappears in the depths.

121804.q: What does an oxygen-free lake bed also release, making the over-fertilisation worse?
121804.e: Without oxygen, phosphate bound to iron dissolves out of the sediment. This internal fertilisation keeps a lake eutrophic for a long time.
121804.m: Without oxygen, the sediment releases phosphate.

121805.q: How does the visibility depth of a lake usually change as the trophic state rises?
121805.e: More nutrients mean more algae, which make the water cloudy. Oligotrophic lakes are therefore usually clearer than eutrophic ones.
121805.m: The richer in nutrients a lake is, the cloudier it usually is.

121806.q: In which canton is Lake Baldegg?
121806.e: Lake Baldegg is in the Hochdorf district. It is one of the lakes of the Swiss Plateau in the north of this canton.
121806.m: Lake Baldegg is in the canton of Lucerne.

121807.q: In which area is Lake Baldegg?
121807.e: This valley stretches north from the Lucerne area. It is named after its lakes (“See” means lake).
121807.m: Lake Baldegg is in the Seetal.

121808.q: Into which lake does the water of Lake Baldegg flow via the Aabach stream?
121808.e: The Aabach links Lake Baldegg with Lake Hallwil, which lies lower down. Both lakes suffered from heavy over-fertilisation.
121808.m: The Aabach flows from Lake Baldegg to Lake Hallwil.

121809.q: Which nature conservation organisation owns Lake Baldegg?
121809.e: Lake Baldegg belongs to Pro Natura. This makes it one of the few Swiss lakes owned by a nature conservation organisation.
121809.m: Lake Baldegg belongs to Pro Natura.

121810.q: Why does Lake Baldegg have to be aerated artificially?
a: Because of over-fertilisation, the deep water lacks oxygen
The lake water is too salty
Fish need air bubbles to breathe
Otherwise the lake would freeze every winter
121810.e: Many algae die and sink to the bottom, where their breakdown uses up oxygen. Since the early 1980s, air and oxygen have therefore been pumped into the lake.
121810.m: Lake Baldegg is aerated because its deep water lacks oxygen.

121811.q: What is the main cause of the over-fertilisation of Lake Baldegg?
a: Phosphorus from farming in the catchment area
121811.e: There is a lot of livestock farming with slurry in the catchment area. Phosphorus gets into the lake from it and boosts algal growth.
121811.m: Phosphorus from farming over-fertilises Lake Baldegg.

121812.q: Why is aerating a lake, as at Lake Baldegg, regarded as only treating the symptoms?
a: It does not reduce the input of nutrients from the catchment area
121812.e: Aeration supplies oxygen to the deep water but does not remove the cause. The only lasting help is to let less phosphorus into the lake.
121812.m: Aeration eases the effects but not the cause of over-fertilisation.

121813.q: Which two methods are combined when aerating lakes such as Lake Baldegg?
a: Help with mixing in winter and adding oxygen in summer
Breaking ice in winter and liming in summer
Pumping out in winter and dredging in summer
Chlorinating in winter and shading in summer
121813.e: In winter, air blown in helps the whole lake to mix. In summer, oxygen is added directly to the deep water without destroying the stratification.
121813.m: Lake aeration helps mixing in winter and brings oxygen into the depths in summer.

a: The water research institute of the ETH Domain
A fisheries authority of the canton of Zurich
121814.e: Eawag researches water in all its aspects, from lakes to waste water. Like Empa, the PSI and the WSL, it belongs to the ETH Domain.
121814.m: Eawag is the water research institute of the ETH Domain.

121815.e: Eawag’s headquarters are in Dübendorf in the canton of Zurich. It has a second site near Lucerne.
121815.m: Eawag has its headquarters in Dübendorf.

121816.q: On which lake is Eawag’s second site in Kastanienbaum?
121816.e: In Kastanienbaum near Lucerne, Eawag runs its centre for lake and fish research. The site lies directly on Lake Lucerne.
121816.m: Eawag carries out research in Kastanienbaum on Lake Lucerne.

121817.q: What did the German abbreviation Eawag originally stand for?
a: Federal Institute for Water Supply, Wastewater Treatment and Water Protection
European Agency for Water and Waters
Federal Office for Hydraulic Engineering and Glaciers
121817.e: The name shows the three core topics: drinking water, waste water and protecting waters. Today only the abbreviation Eawag is used as a name.
121817.m: Eawag does research on drinking water, waste water and protecting waters.

121818.q: In which decade was Eawag’s forerunner founded as an advisory office of ETH?
121818.e: Eawag started in 1936 as an ETH advisory office for waste water treatment and drinking water supply. Later it became an independent research institute.
121818.m: Eawag has its roots in the 1930s.

121819.q: Which simple method of disinfecting drinking water with sunlight in PET bottles did Eawag promote?
121819.e: With SODIS, clear PET bottles filled with water are left in the sun for a few hours. The UV radiation and the heat kill pathogens.

121820.q: Which energy-efficient Eawag building in Dübendorf became known as a model of sustainable building?
121820.e: Forum Chriesbach was moved into in 2006 and manages without conventional heating. It is regarded as a showcase of sustainable architecture.
121820.m: Forum Chriesbach is Eawag’s showcase building.

121821.q: Which Eawag research topic concerns collecting urine separately to recover nutrients?
121821.e: Urine contains a large part of the nutrients in waste water. Eawag developed methods to make fertiliser from it.
121821.m: Fertiliser can be made from separately collected urine.

121822.q: What does the saprobity of a river or stream measure?
121822.e: Saprobity describes how heavily a body of water is polluted with easily degradable organic matter. This is broken down by bacteria, using up oxygen.
121822.m: Saprobity shows the organic pollution of a body of water.

121823.q: In the saprobic system, what is used to determine the water quality of a stream?
a: Indicator organisms living in the stream
The width of the stream bed
121823.e: Some animals and small organisms can only tolerate clean water, others also heavily polluted water. The species found allow conclusions about the pollution.
121823.m: Indicator organisms reveal the water quality.

121824.q: What is the saprobic level for clean, barely polluted water called?
121824.e: Oligosaprobic waters are hardly polluted with organic matter and rich in oxygen. Sensitive species such as stonefly larvae live there.

121825.q: Which animal, as an indicator organism, shows very heavy organic pollution?
121825.e: Tubifex can tolerate very little oxygen and lives in rotting sludge. Mass occurrences point to polysaprobic conditions.
121825.m: Many Tubifex worms indicate heavily polluted water.

121826.q: What does a high saprobic index show for a stream?
121826.e: The higher the index, the more easily degradable organic substances the water contains. Low values stand for clean water.
121826.m: A high saprobic index means heavily polluted water.

121827.q: A sample contains species A (saprobic value 1.5; frequency 3) and species B (saprobic value 2.5; frequency 1). What is the saprobic index?
121827.e: You calculate (1.5 times 3 plus 2.5 times 1) divided by (3 plus 1). That gives 7 divided by 4, so 1.75.
121827.m: The saprobic index is an average weighted by frequency.

121828.q: Which animal indicates clean, oxygen-rich stream water?
121828.e: Stonefly larvae need a lot of oxygen and only occur in clean streams. Tubifex, red midge larvae and water lice tolerate polluted water.
121828.m: Stonefly larvae only live in clean water.

121829.q: What is the difference between saprobity and trophic state?
a: Saprobity measures the breakdown of organic substances, trophic state the production driven by nutrients
Saprobity only applies to lakes, trophic state only to seas
Saprobity measures temperature, trophic state salt content
121829.e: The trophic state describes primary production by plants and algae. Saprobity describes the breakdown of organic matter by bacteria and other decomposers.
121829.m: Trophic state means building up, saprobity means breaking down organic substances.

a: Invertebrates on the bed of a body of water that are visible to the naked eye
Fish that live on the bottom
121830.e: Macrozoobenthos includes insect larvae, snails, mussels, worms and small crustaceans, for example. They live on and in the bed of the water.
121830.m: Macrozoobenthos are the visible invertebrates living on the bottom of waters.

121831.q: Which three insect orders make up the EPT taxa, which are regarded as indicators of good water quality?
121831.e: EPT stands for Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera and Trichoptera. Many of their larvae need clean, oxygen-rich water.
121831.m: Many EPT larvae indicate clean water.

121832.q: How can you recognise the larvae of many caddisflies particularly easily?
a: By a case they build themselves from small stones or plant parts
By a hard lime shell with a lid
121832.e: Caddisfly larvae stick sand, small stones or plant parts together with silk to make a case. In it they protect their soft abdomen.
121832.m: Caddisfly larvae build themselves a case.

121833.q: Where do the larvae of mayflies and stoneflies live?
a: In the water of streams and lakes
In the wood of dead trees
In the flowers of meadow plants
121833.e: The larvae of these insects develop in water, often under stones. Only the adults fly on land.
121833.m: Mayfly and stonefly larvae live in water.

121834.q: Why are insect larvae on the stream bed counted to assess water quality?
a: Many species can only tolerate clean water
Larvae only live in polluted water
121834.e: Sensitive species disappear when the water is polluted. Which animals are present therefore shows the water quality over a longer period.
121834.m: Bottom-dwelling animals in a stream indicate the water quality.

121835.q: Which feeding group of the macrozoobenthos mainly shreds leaves that have fallen into the water?
121835.e: Shredders such as freshwater shrimps and some caddisfly larvae eat fallen leaves. In this way they make the energy from the trees on the bank usable for the water.
121835.m: Shredders eat leaves that have fallen into the water.

121836.q: Which group of animals does the freshwater shrimp Gammarus belong to?
121836.e: The freshwater shrimp is an amphipod and therefore a crustacean. Despite its German name “Bachflohkrebs” (stream flea crab), it is not related to fleas.
121836.m: The freshwater shrimp is a crustacean.

121837.q: What is it called when bottom-dwelling animals are carried off by the current, which often increases at night?
121837.e: Many invertebrates let go of the bottom and drift downstream. This drift mainly happens in the dark, when fish can see them less well.
121837.m: Drift is bottom-dwelling animals being carried off by the current.

121838.q: What causes hydropeaking (surge and low flow) in a river?
a: Storage power plants being switched on and off
121838.e: Storage power plants mainly produce electricity when demand is high. Then the flow below the outlet rises sharply and afterwards falls again.
121838.m: Hydropeaking is caused by the operation of storage power plants.
